He is taking back now a good deal of what he stated. In fact I am afraid that when on his feet the hon. member really states' things that in his calmer moments he would regret. Some of these witnesses, when cross questioned, admitted that they could not swear whether this man had been on his farm or not. One of the gentlemen referred is Levasseur. This was his total examination:
Q. You are living on a farm, Mr. Levasseur?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. How far from Beaubien's place?
A. Two miles.
Q. Do you remember Mr. Beaubien being in residence there since 1910?
A. X used to stay home and he lived two miles from me.
Q. Had you occasion to go by the place?
A. No.
Q. Then you could not tell me whether he lived there or not?
A. No.
That is the total examination of one of the witnesses for Arguin and still the hon. member quotes this man as one of the witnesses to bear out the statement of Arguin in regard to Beaubien's residence. From the evidence of other witnesses I could quote much the same all the way through if I wanted to take up the time of the House, but I think I have quoted sufficient to impress at least the fair minded members that the hon. gentleman exceeded his duties entirely in drawing upon his imagination rather than relying on the facts as stated in this report of the investigation. He states that the deputy minister really approved of this and recommended it because it was recommended by Cuttle, the inspector of agencies, who conducted the investigation, was on the ground and was in a better position to judge than we are here. 1 do not desire to screen myself behind any officials of the department. I realize my responsibility as head of the department; but, at the same time not knowing the details myself, having had an investigation conducted by a gentleman in whose impartiality honour and integrity I have every confidence, notwithstanding the scurrilous names applied to him by the hon. member for Moosejaw to-day in a manner that was unworthy of the hon. gentleman, when the deputy minister coincided in the view of the commissioner that no matter what doubt there might be as to the completeness of Beaubien's residence under the circumstances it would be a shame- that in effect is their report-to drive Beaubien from the land, I concurred in that decision.
I notice that he tried to make a point by stating that this cold-hearted man had driven Arguin, with his wife and family, out on the concession lines. Now, Arguin's own residence, where he had been living all the time previous to going over to Beaubien's farm, was only on the adjoining^ quarter-section, so he had not far to go to reach his home. As soon as Beaubien went away Arguin seized the opportunity, left his own home on the adjoining quarter-section, and moved over to Beaubien's, though the land laws did not require him to do so. Residence on the adjoining quarter-section was all that was necessary in order to secure a patent for this pre-emption, but in order to qualify a little more strongly, he moved over to Beaubien's pre-emption. When Arguin was turned out, as the hon. member states he was, he was at perfect liberty to go into residence on his own farm as heretofore. Mr. Beaubien had upwards of 115

acres under cultivation, and, having given the evidence he had as to the reasons for his absence, the department considered that sufficient to reinstate him in his entry, which they accordingly did; and I do not think any impartial member in this House or anybody in the country would condemn the Government for restoring that entry after all that cultivation had been done, and after he had performed his duties as to fencing and residence-although perhaps he did not live on the homestead all the time with his family; he did not say he did so. Although the hon. gentleman stated that there was not a tittle of evidence as to this man's bona fide residence, he afterwards referred to the fact that Beaubien had sworn that he was in residence, and the hon. member said that Beaubien's evidence was false; in other words, that it meant nothing at all. There were other affidavits sent in, prior to this investigation, by friends of Beaubien-gentlemen of repute in Gravelbourg who went to prove that Beaubien was in actual residence on his land. The hon. gentleman ignores that, but the department cannot afford to ignore it. Certainly somebody has been telling an untruth, but at any rate a great many of those witnesses on whom the hon. gentleman is relying, when cross-examined, could not swear that Beaubien did not reside on his farm, and in view of that we thought -and thought justly-that Beaubien's entry should be restored. I do not think our action has created any irritation in that part of the country except perhaps amongst some hard-headed Liberal friends of hon. gentlemen opposite. The general public, so far as my knowledge goes, believe that the man who should be in possession of the land is now in possession of it. The hon. member also made a point about Beaubien's handing the land over to his son. That is not at all contrary to the land laws. When Beaubien's entry was restored, the effect of that was to terminate the cancellation proceedings. His entry was in good standing, and he had a perfect right to transfer it to his son who was about to leave for Montana to take up land. He naturally desired to keep his son in the neighbourhood, and therefore transferred his land to him. That is a matter of almost every-day occurrence, and is quite in accordance with the regulations of the department. It is something that I think should be encouraged. When a father has sufficient land of his own to set up his sons, I do not see any harm 
in his doing that. I do not wish to take up the time of the House in dealing with this matter any further because, after all, I realize that it is not a case that should be discussed here on amendments to the Land Act. Grievances like this should be brought up when we are in Supply. This grievance was aired on one occasion when my Estimates were before the House, and I think the hon. gentleman might have waited till the Estimates came up again, and not have blocked the passing of legislation that is bound to be-at least I think so-in the interests of the western farmers. Other statements have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite. The hon. member for Medicine Hat spoke about receiving petitions to the effect that the holders of preemptions desired to get their land absolutely free like their homesteads. A number of those petitions came into the department, also petitions of quite a different character. As I stated when I moved the second reading of this Bill the other evening, representations of various kinds have been made to me. One proposal was to refund the interest that had been paid. It is an involved question and a very important one, and after giving it my very best consideration, I came to the conclusion that the Government could not come down to Parliament and ask for the refunding of this money, paid in whole or in part, which would run up to over $2,000,000. I thought that was an unreasonable request, and, under the circumstances, I thought the best I could do would	be to	recommend that thethree	years'	interest should	for
the future be thrown off. That was the first request made to me by the holders Of pre-emptions when I was out in the West last summer; but their requests have gradually become more drastic ini character, I came to the conclusion that inasmuch as a man could qualify for his homestead at the end of three years, and while the present law provides that he shall be charged interest on his pre-emption for the first three yeaTS-though he is not allowed to pay any portion of interest or principal-that it was only right that the farmers should be relieved of interest during those thiree years. The member for Medicine Hat, I understand, was in favour of shortening up the time within which pre-emption patents could be secured. That is another request that has been made to the department, and I have endeavoured to meet the wishes of those who were desirous

of getting their pre-emption patents at the same time as the homestead patents. I know the hardships they .are labouring under out there. It may have been a questionable proceeding to have ever instituted this pre-emptioni area; in fact, a great many people now resident in the West say that it was a mistake to have ever allowed pre emptions. Much of that land is not fit for cultivation. In some portions-perhaps a limited area.-once the sod is turned up you cannot get even grass to grow. It is only fit for ranching, and I think that land like that should never have been thrown open for pre-emptions. I agree with the farmers who take exception to the large pre-emption area which has been created, by reason of the fact that much of that land has been represented to me as not fit for cultivation at all, and as only suitable for grazing. It would be no use imposing additional cultivation on those farmers, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat suggested. Before they get the preemption patent they have to cultivate fifty acres more than in the case of a homestead. This Bill provides that they may prove up for their pre-emptions at the end of three years, or as soon thereafter as they can pay for the pre-emption (less the interest, for the three years), and have done the necessary residential and cultivation duties. I think that is as long a step as we can take at the present time. The hon. gentleman also quoted from a letter which he received from a gentleman who took exception to shortening up the time in which they could prove up. This gentleman insisted on a longer residence as otherwise the land holders were .likely to return to the United States. I do not think there is any likelihood of that. We have to compete just now with the United States land laws, which have recently been considerably relaxed. They are striving to get our people over there by allowing them what they call ' enlarged ' homesteads of 320 acres, whereas formerly only 160 acres were allowed. They are also stipulating for three years' residence instead of five, as formerly. 1 think I am therefore justified in bringing in this Bill to relax the existing regulations in our pre-emption area. Far from having received complaints in regard to this Bill, I have received numerous letters quite to the contrary. Far from complaints coming to the department regarding this proposed Bill, I have
received numerous letters to the contrary. One enthusiastic pre-emption holder has written to me that after perusing the provisions of the Bill he would not want one word changed. He said -that it was suitable to the holders of pre-emptions in the West. There may be differences of opinion and there may be petitions as the hon. gentleman states, but on the whole I think that the Bill will give fairly general satisfaction.
In Tegard to what the hon. member from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has stated about the desirability of changing our land laws to meet the changed conditions, all I have to say is that I agree with him and that is the reason I am introducing this Bill, but when he answered the very cogent question put to him by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) as to how he explained the falling off in the number of homestead entries from 1906 to 1908, I did not take very much stock in the explanation that he gave, namely, that it was by reason of the fact of one man being allowed to blanket a number of entries. From 1902 to 1903 the entries dropped by 5,000. I am sure that my hon. friend from Edmonton would be the last to claim that this decline was due to the actions of the Government of those days. In two years' time, between 1906 and 1908 the number of homestead entries fell off more than they have fallen off in the last two year-. They fell off to the extent of 11,450. I do not attribute it to the blanketing process which my hon. friend states was in existence for some years. But I rather attribute it, and I am charitable- enough to give the late Government the benefit of this opinion, to the very same considerations that have caused the homestead entries to fall off in the last two years. In times of financial stringency, we have a lessening of business credit and activity, of necessity agricultural developments will be held in check, just the same as industrial development, -and during those two years there were some 10,000 less homestead entries than there were in 1911. History is repeating itself. How do those ' conditions differ from those of 1906 to 1908? At that time there was, as I have said, a considerable falling off in the number of homestead entries. The falling off in the last two years is not due to any inherent policy on the part of the present Government because there has not been any departure with regard to the land laws up to the present time. The people of Europe, the British Isles and on the American side of the boundary are not aware of any terrorizing process that may have been going on

here before they have come to the country to make their homestead entries. It is useless to attribute to the homestead inspectors or to any officials of the Department of the Interior the falling off in the number of homestead entries.
I am not going to enter into any acrimonious political discussion in Tegard to the various actions of the homestead and other inspectors of the Government in connection with elections, but I desire to give my personal experience of the officials of the late Government and I do not know that conditions differed from those which were found in my own constituency. Well do I remember that I was contesting my seat against the Liberal homestead inspector who had resigned his position shortly before nomination day in order to contest the seat against me and he used his position in the interval to secure the political support at a certain poll of a large section of foreigners who did not know the law of the land and who w'ere terrorized into casting their votes in favour of my opponent. A (homestead inspector was there and he herded these foreigners in a room where a supporter of mine heard everything that took place and this inspector told them that if they desired to get their patents for their homesteads they would have to vote for my political opponent. They lined up next day under the auspices of this homestead inspector who was at the poll, assisted hy a gentleman sent out by the Immigration Department from Winnipeg. This latter gentleman was not allowed at the poll because he went out on the train on Saturday. A warrant was out for his arrest for bribery in another constituency and a policeman was sent to escort him back to the city of Winnipeg.
Hear, hear.
Was he terrorizing them with two-dollar bills?
He did not get a chance, because the officers took the money from him and kept it under lock and key until after election day. He did not have time to get it in circulation.

Was he scaring them
badly?

No, they were not scared by that. But it showed the estimate placed on the purchasable vote when they divided this money up into two-dollar bills. There was another gentleman, a mounted policeman, sent out from, the city of Regina. I am sorry that the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is not in his place. That right hon. gentleman, when the fact was brought to his attention, denied that there were any mounted policemen in connection with the Department of the Interior, but I proved to his own satisfaction that there were certain mounted policemen associated with the forestry branch of the Department of the Interior. This gentleman, who was sent out iby the then Minister of the Interior, took his position at the door of the polling booth, wearing his side arms in order to terrorize *the people who had come from countries where compulsory military service was in vogue, and to convince them that if they did not vote against myself there would be military conscription in this country.
After the arrest on Sunday in Winnipeg of the gentleman to whom I have referred, a telegram was sent on Monday to the Yorkton-office and another interpreter came down to take the place of the man who had been taken into custody. He stood at the door of the poll with two other officials of the Government, and by reason of the efforts of these Government officials the result of the vote cast in that one'poll was 112 for my opponent and eight for your humble servant. I give this as an instance, not to justify anything that might Ibe wrong in connection with the officials of the present Government, but to show how badly it comes from a member of the late Government to accuse the homestead inspectors and officials of the Government of terrorizing the people in the West. Terrorism-they do not know the meaning of the term.
They are learning it.

I hope they do learn it in some respects, at any rate, not that I admit that there is any terrorizing done. The gentlemen who have been accused oif terrorizing have no reason to claim that

they have not been informed as to what their duties are. I have pointed out to them their duties, and I have told them that the department will not tolerate any activity in elections. At the same time, I think St is only fair to say, that the charges which have been made on the floor of this House have been refuted by these men.
I do not mean to take up the time of the House in order to go any more lengthily into that phase of the question, but I just wish to say a word in regard to the charges which are being made about the departure from the past policy. There is a departure from the past policy tout it is a departure for the better. The homestead inspectors are doing their duty and they are making thousands and thousands more inspections [DOT] than were made by the homestead inspectors when the Liberals were in power.
Not at election times.
Yes, at all times.
Does the minister ever read their diaries?

No, I have not read their diaries, but I have read the reports of their inspections. They state that there are so many demands in connection with proving on homesteads that there are not sufficient homestead inspectors to keep up with the work.
In reply to the remarks of my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Ailcins) about water-powers, I may tell him that I realize the importance of that branch of the department. There is a very great deal of force indeed in what the hon. gentleman has stated. The Winnipeg river is a river of vast water-powers, and it is the intention of the Government to conserve them. The hon. gentleman may have been a little misled in regard to the water-powers that still remain vested in the Crown. My information from the head official of that branch is that at least fifty per cent of the available water-powers on that river are still vested in the Crown, and those that were alienated were not alienated by this Government, but by the preceding Government. It is a question as to whether we are prepared to go in for Government ownership and operation of water-powers. I do not know whether we are that far advanced; I do not think we are at the present time, but I can see the propriety and the wisdom of conserving these powers and not allowing them to get into private hands for exploitation. I can assure hon. gentlemen that at the present time all the powers on the Winnipeg river-are reserved and will not be disposed of. There have 211
of course been applications from private capitalists for these water-powers, with stipulations that they would erect pulp mills of large capacity on that river. But, after consulting Judge Robson, the Utility Commissioner for Manitoba appointed by the provincial Government, who is opposed to the alienation of any of these water-powers, I thought it wise to carry out his recommendation.
I trust that this Bill shall receive the sympathetic consideration of hon. gentlemen. I do not wish to encourage any debate that would lead us away from the due consideration of its various provisions, but I felt called upon to defend myself when such serious accusations were made against the management of the department as were made this afternoon.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Blain in the Chair.

Before the House rose at six o'clock my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior had replied to some extent to the arguments which I had made with regard to the Gravelbourg homestead. The minister then proceeded to discuss the general merits of his Bill, and I had not an opportunity to reply before these other remarks had intervened. I had purposely refrained from taking up the time of the committee in the way of quoting evidence; but my hon. friend the minister went out of his way to quote some of the evidence, and I do not propose to allow it to stand as he has put it, namely: that the evidence has failed to establish what I have stated. Therefore I purpose putting on ' Hansard ' a few references and exact quotations from the evidence to show that what I have said is correct.
My hon. friend in the first place referred to the witness who said that he could not swear that Mr. Beaubien was not on his homestead at any certain date. The weakness of my hon. friend's case is manifest in such an argument because it is impossible to establish a negative of this kind. The witness in question, whose name is Levasseur, was able to say only that he had lived in Gravelbourg, and that Mr. Beaubien lived there also. On crossexamination he, of course, could not state any certain date on which he was in Gravelbourg, and he could not swear to any certain date on which Beaubien was not on the homestead. All that he could do, and all that any of these witnesses could



do, was to establish that the home of Mr. Beaubien and his family was in Gravel-bourg during the years to which I have referred. On page 4 of the evidence, in the examination of this same witness, there appear the following question and answer:
Q. As far as you know, he lived there?
A. Yes sir, in the village.
No man living can prove that any one is in default in his homestead duties if he has to give the day and the date; but reputable citizens swore that Mr. Beaubien, to their certain knowledge, had his permanent home in the town.

I submit that the
hen. gentleman is not speaking to the question before the House. He is entirely out of order, and we may as well proceed to discuss this Bill. We might keep on all night discussing matters that are not relevant, and I think it would be just as well if you, Sir, would hold the hon. gentleman down to the question before the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope the hon. member for Moosejaw will confine his remarks as much as possible to the Bill.

The point of
order is very badly taken at this moment. Possibly it would have been a good time to take it when my hon. friend originally introduced the question; but, the question having been introduced and discussed very fully by my hon. friend from Moosejaw, and having been replied to equally fully by the Minister of the Interior, it seems to me that the point of order is taken a little tardily, to say the least. My hon. friend is a little slow in his movements.

The hon. member
from Moosejaw having discussed the question so fully and the minister having replied, our duty is to proceed with the discussion of the Bill. I am not asking that any privileges be taken away from the hon. member for Moosejaw or from the hon. Minister of the Interior. They have both had their say. I rather think the point raised by my hon. friend from Red Deer is not well taken.

I am perfectly sure my hon. friend from Hal-ton will be as dispassionate as myself in a desire to arrive at correct conclusions. I wish to submit to his extremely lucid and impartial intellect the statement that the hon. member from Moosejaw is at present engaged in
[Mr. Knowles. 1
stating that the hon. Minister of the Interior has quoted parts of certain evidence. The hon. member for Moosejaw goes on to state that other parts of the evidence, not quoted iby the Minister of the Interior, go to contradict the parts of the evidence that have been quoted by the Minister of the Interior. I submit to my hon. friend from Halton the consideration that he and I, having this desire to bring a lucid and dispassionate consideration to the full evidence, are bound to allow my hon. friend from Moosejaw to quote the evidence which he says absolutely refutes and disproves the evidence already quoted by the Minister of the Interior.
And neither had anything to do with the question.
Is it possible to discuss the point of order without permission from the Chair?

Always in
order, I understand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it is always in order for any member to rise to a point of order, and discussion is allowed.

When I first rose, I intended to refer to a few portions of the evidence, but now I intend to refer to more of it. If my hon. friend from Halton wastes much more of my time, I will perhaps read the whole business.

I rise to a point of order. I certainly was not wasting the time of the hon. member for Moosejaw. I rose to a question that I had a perfect right to rise to, and my hon. friend has no right to charge me with interfering with his time. The fact of the matter is that he is interfering with the time of the House.

I rise to a point of
order. There is no point of order before the House. I have the floor.
Mr, HENDERSON: I rose to a point of order on account of the reference that the hon. member for Moosejaw made to myself. When I get through with that, then the hon. member will have the floor. I did not understand, Mr. Chairman, that you had decided that the hon. member for Moosejaw could discuss whether the moon was made of green cheese or any other question outside of that before the House. I submit that the hon. member should confine himself to the question and that you, Sir, should ask him to do so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have already asked the hon. member for Moosejaw to confine his remarks to the Bill. I hope that the hon. gentlemen taking part in this discussion will assist the Chair in keeping order and expediting business.

I take your request in all kindness, Mr. Chairman, but I do not think it is needed. The first reference which I wish to make is to page 15 of the evidence, where Mr. Dureault distinctly says that Mr. Beaubien's residence was in Gravelbourg. I quote the following from Mr. Dureault's evidence:
Q. Tou are acquainted with Mr. J. N. Beau-bien?-A. Yes.
Q. Where does he live?-A. In town.
Q. The town of Gravelbourg?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Does he live in the town of Gravelbourg with his family?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. How many years have you been carrying on a business in the town of Gravelbourg? A. Two years in May.
<4. During the time you have carried on your business in Gravelbourg was Mr. Beau-bien also carrying on business?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. During all the time?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. His family resided with him in town ?- A. Yes, sir.
Q. Can you see from your own place the house or place of business of Mr. Beaubien? -A. Yes, sir.
This merchant, who lived just across the street, testified that Mr. Beaubien carried on business in Gravelbourg and that he lived there with his family. On page 20 the following evidence is given by Mr. Gray manager of the Union Bank of Canada at Gravelbourg:
Q. You are manager of the Union bank in Gravelbourg?-A. Yes.
Q. How long have you been there?-A. Three years-going on three years.
Turning to page 22 we find the following:
Q. She has been residing there ever since you have been in Gravelbourg?-A. That I cannot say. To the best of my knowledge and belief they have.
In a small place like Gravelbourg everybody knows where everybody else lives, and this evidence that to the best of the witness's knowledge and belief Mrs. Beaubien had been doing business there is sufficiently conclusive.
On page 30 Mr. McKay, manager of the Bank of Toronto, gives the following evidence :
Q. You know Mrs. Beaubien and the children?.-A. Yes, sir.
Q. And you lived just across the street?- A Yes, sir.
Q. And you are in a position to say that while you were in Gravelbourg Mr. Beaubien 211*
and his family lived just across the street?_
Yes, sir.
The evidence of Mr. Hamlin, Government telegraph operator, employed by the Department of Public Works, may be found on page 33. I quote the following:
Q. How long have you been here?-A. I have been here three years at the end of this month or at the end of May.
Q. During that time he kept a boarding house in Gravelbourg-any other business?- A. A store and a butcher shop.
Q. During all that time were you boarding at his place?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Who was the housekeeper and who looked after the table?-A. Mr. Beaubien's daughters and Mrs. Beaubien, as far as I know.
Q. Mr. Beaubien and his family lived in the village at the boarding house?-A. As far as I know, yes sir. -
This is the evidence of a telegraph operator who boarded at that very house, and had been in Gravelbourg' for three years. My hon. friend endeavoured to produce as evidence of Mr. Beaubien's having been in residence the fact that one of his witnesses would not swear that for three years he had not resided seven weeks each year on his homestead. The minister can produce no other case where such residence has been regarded as sufficient. I did not say that there was evidence that Beaubien had never lived on his homestead; I did say that there was no evidence of his bona fide residence upon it. A bona fide homesteader is one who lives on the homestead with his wife and children. The facts are so indisputably uncontradicted that the efforts of Beaubien to prove that he did live upon the land with his wife and family show that he is a falsifier. I repeat what I have already said: that the minister gave the homestead to a man who could not show that he was entitled to it, and in so doing he committed a great injustice.
The minister dwelt upon the fact that Arguin resided on the quarter:section. He went there because he had so little faith in the minister's officers that he wanted to establish his position beyond peradventure and to get into residence on the quarter-section. Time after time, in writing to the minister, Arguin said that it was doubtful whether he would be able to secure a square deal, and that he was afraid that there would be false reports. Such a report was made by a man named Erratt. Let me say, in passing, that Mr. Cuttle never called on Beaubien to give a single bit of evidence; Beaubien himself had to be called by Arguin. The whole burden of proving the negative was put upon Arguin,
[DOT]3344

and, even with that burden, the merits of the ease are entirely on his side. At page 102 -Mr. Beaubien is asked:
Q. Do you know Mr. W. H. Erratt who used [DOT]to be homestead inspector?
A. Yes, I know him, I remember him.
Q. Did you go to your land with him.
A. Yes, X came up from Moosejaw with him.
The fact is that he went to Moosejaw, got the homestead inspector and brought him to the homestead to make this partisan report. The inspector who, at the beck and call of political tools, drives 80 miles to a homestead for the purpose of doing special inspection work, and then reports, the evidence to the contrary notwithstanding, that the man has been in residence; that inspector is neglecting his legitimate duties and subjecting himself to the undue influence of the person for whom he makes such a report. This condition of affairs, on the face of it, is indicative of improper relationship between this politcal tool and the homestead inspector. If the former Minister of the Interior, the hon. member for Edmonton, had been in office and this matter had come to his knowledge, the homestead inspector would have had a very short shrift for his position.
At the time of the taking of the evidence from which my horn friend is quoting, who was in possession?
Arguin.

Beaubien owned the land in the first place, as I understand it, and this man Arguin was what they call a claim jumper. I have been in camps where he would have been shot on sight for jumping another man's property.
My hon. friend has yet a great deal to learn. What he calls claim jumpers are among our best citizens.
I have no doubt about that.

I do not think the
minister will contradict me when I say that one-half of our homesteaders are claim jumpers. I think that is correct that they have entered for homestead which they have secured in the same way as Arguin has secured this by applying to have cancellation proceedings commenced. Tens of thousands of the best citizens we have, and my hon. friend, without knowing anything about it, goes out of his way to cast a slur on them.

The only case of this kind that came to my notice was that of a gentleman who was taken ill with typhoid and his wife took him to the hospital. The time expired while he was in the hospital, and they lost the house and farm and the labour of years. I consider that if such a law is relaxed a little in case of sickness or disability to be on the land, there is nothing wrong with it; but I have not much use for a man who has lots of property for himself and a homestead of his own who tries to jump another man's claim.
My hon. friend should not be so harsh on this man, because he does not know much about it. My hon. friend is quite at sea in the matter.

I am looking at the
ethical side of it.

My hon. friend will take my word for it that he is wrong. In conclusion, I would call attention to the fact that there was an improper relationship between Erratt and Beaubien. I think the minister will agree that when we were able to establish out of the mouth of Beaubien himself that he went in to Moosejaw and brought out the homestead inspector, we have established a prima facie case for suspicion. The minister argues that because Beaubien was cancelled and Arguin entered and then Arguin cancelled and Beaubien restored, that wiped out and abandoned the cancellation proceedings. The minister should be careful in what he says. Will he lay it down as a departmental ruling that an application for cancellation is to be removed because it has been successful and then its success has been taken away from the man? Will he lay it down as a departmental ruling that I can get my homestead in good standing by allowing cancellation to go through and then have the cancellation withdrawn, and that I will then be better off than I was before? The minister cannot mean that. If there was a new entry and another flO paid, it might be a different matter. Surely all that was done was that Arguin was cancelled and there was a restoration to the original condition of affairs. I cannot believe the minister is serious in saying that in restoring Beaubien there was, ipso facto, an abandonment of the cancellation proceedings. If that is so, if things were restored to their former conditions, then the cancellation proceedings were outstanding

against Beaubien until he put himself in good standing by doing at least thirty days residence, and according to the law of Canada he could not be allowed to abandon in favour of his son. There is no need to labour that point, it is too clear. Somebody has slipped there in his anxiety to help out Beaubien the better and put this poor fellow on the street, and has overlooked the fact that all the restoration did was to restore things to their former position. The Postmaster General was not here when I stated that Beaubien said he.saw him about this matter in Moosejaw last summer. Does the minister remember seeing a man named Beaubien who spoke about a homestead this summer?
Put your question in writing and I will think over it.

I dare say he did see the minister. I do not know whether he came to Ottawa and saw the Prime Minister or not, but he seems to have looked after the Cabinet pretty well. I do not say it is because of that fact, but the result is that the man has the land. Let me tell the minister that his administration has become in very bad odour out there. I have not said anything against Cuttle other than what I find in this file. The minister has brought out a great many general charges about Liberals. In the first place that has nothing to do with this matter and he has not the record. I have the record here for what I have to say and it is this we are concerned with. The minister is asking us to change his Dominion Lands Act and we want, before we entrust him with other powers and a new condition of affairs, to tell him what we think of his management of western lands under the present law. There is a growing want of confidence in the honesty and integrity of the administration of the lands in the West. The minister has had homestead inspectors who were a disgrace to the department. He has had to fire many of them. He has had land agents whom he has had to fire because they played the game too coarsely. Do not let him think that I am talking about something that does not exist. I have 130,000 or 140,000 constituents. I say that I believe on my soul their ownership of their homesteads is not safe and that they are not getting a square deal in the homestead office at Moosejaw. I made my charge against Beaubien and I proved it and I may have more definite charges to make about officials in the land office and how good money looks to them before I
am through. If the minister thinks that everything is going on well in the West he is in a fool's paradise. The people do not think it. The homestead inspectors are not doing their work. We have one man there who was appointed homestead inspector. He hung around for a while and then they wanted him to do some work. He said: why, I worked before the elections, you do not expect me to work now do you? By and by he quit because they insisted on his doing some work. The people are not getting any service ait all. When I read to the minister the diaries of men who go for ten days without doing anything^ he must know that they are not doing their work. I have here a letter from a poor fellow who has been trying to get $160 refunded on his improvements. Such a refund would be everything to him, more than $50,000 to the minister. He has applied for an order to get the money, the minister's instructions have been out for nearly a year to get the homestead inspector to make a report on these improvements so that the man could get the money. I put the question on the Order Paper: When was an inspection ordered? The answer was that it was ordered on the 5th of April, 1913, and on the 23rd of April of this year there had been no inspection. Question No. 5 was: Has the homestead inspector's report been received? The minister's answer was:
A. No. The land is situated north of the south Saskatchewan river and the homestead inspector recently explained that on account of weather and the state of the roads it has been practically impossible to do any work in that country for some time, but that he would make his report as soon after first of the month as weather and roads would permit.
On the* same file in regard to the same man there are three letters signed by the minister. Here is one last summer saying: I am writing to have the inspector make a report. The inspectors treat the minister like a nonentity, saying that the weather is bad and the roads are bad. They reply to the minister: when we get good roads we will go and inspect. The man wrote finally to the minister and got a reply on the 27th of October. He was honoured with an autograph signature of the minister.
My dear Sir,-I am in receipt of your letter of the 15th instant, with regard to the improvements placed by you on the S.W. \ of 3,23,12, W. 3rd meridian, when you held entry for the same.
In reply I beg to say that instructions were given on the 3rd instant, to have a homestead inspector make a careful valuation of the improvements placed on this land by you, and in view of your recent communication, further instructions have now been given to have

this valuation made at the earliest possible date. As soon as the inspector's report is received you will be further advised.
Tours faithfully,

I must say to the credit of the minister that his mistake as to the date mentioned in this letter was unintentional. The minister states that instructions were given on the 3rd inst. What he should have said was that instructions were given several months ago; they were given away back in May, nearly six months before he wrote this letter. I come to another letter dated January 23, 1914-no homestead inspector's report yet.
My dear Sir,-I am in receipt of your lettei of the .15th instant, with regard to the south west J of section 3, township 23, range 12,, west of the 3rd meridian.
In reply, I regret very much that you have suffered any inconvenience on account of the delay in the department in dealing with this case, but I may assure you that most explicit instructions have been given to have the homestead inspector make the required report at once, and also that the report is to be forwarded here as soon as made. When this report is received in the department your request will be dealt with as promptly as possible, and you will be fully advised as to what action the department can take.
Tours faithfully,
W. J. Roche.
H. R. McVeigh, Esq.,
Outlook, Sask.
Is it not remarkable that any member of the Government can ivait as calmly in his office at Ottawa as the minister did from October till the 23rd of January of the following year, after having given explicit instructions for a report to be made at once? But that was not all. This man wrote and re-wrote, and on February 10 the minister sent him the following letter:
My dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 3rd instant, in which you point out that you have not been advised of the decision of the department in regard to the south west \ of section 3, township 3 range 12, west of the 3rd Meridian.
In reply, I beg to inform you that the homestead inspector's report has not as yet been received. I am wiring the agent to have the matter attended to at once.
Tours faithfully,
W. J. Roche. .
Is not that a funny way to serve the people of Canada? After reading all the pathetic letters this man wrote, the minister s heart was touched, and he sent him $50 to keep him from starving, although the man was entitled to $145 or $165, I forget which. Fancy a minister of the Crown taking such disobedience from his Homestead Inspector, and writing such
£Mr. Knowles.]
letters saying ' I assure you I have given explicit instructions,' etc. The minister might just as well have written: I am doing the best I can, but the homestead inspector tells me to go plumb to the mischief; for that is what it amounts to. Imagine a homestead inspector saying to the minister: When the weather is pleasant and the roads are nice I will go out and make the report, but till then you can hold your horses. It is time the minister put his foot down and let his homestead inspectors know he is boss; let them realize that they are there to do their work honestly and not for political purposes; that their duty is to serve the men that are making that country and Canada -not the men on the patronage list or friends of the Government, but the man behind the pair of oxen breaking up the sod on the homestead; and that they are not appointed to send back silly answers to the minister, after a year has gone by, that when the weather is pleasant and the roads are nice they will make a report. I care not how honest the minister may be in his own mind, he must take the responsibility, and my message to my constituents is that they have very little to hope for from the minister and the Government of Canada, and from the lazy political heelers landed in those Government jobs in Saskatchewan.

I just want to speak for a minute or two along the line my hon. friend from Moosejaw has taken. I have made the statement that the administration of the Department of the Interior is not conducive to the development of the country, and I just want to give one instance. Hitherto the practice has been to sell land which has been withdrawn from reservation by auction after public notice. This case relates to the southeast quarter of 16-25-5-W., 5th meridian, which is just a little west of Calgary. I will give a brief sketch of the return which was brought down relating to that piece of land. On April 21, 1902, C. E. Sibbald applied to enter for this land. He was informed that the land was under reservation as a water reserve. Some years passed, and finally the country around was fairly well settled. During the late Administration there were several applications for entry for this particular section. On January 15, 1908. Mr. J. A. W. Fraser was informed by myself, when he applied for homestead rights, that the land would have to be sold by auction. On January 24, 1908, Mr. MAY 6, 1914
Pereira wrote another applicant, called McDougal, that the land when withdrawn would be sold by auction. On July 15, 1911, an order was issued by the department to have the land inspected for withdrawal. Apparently the inspector did not make the inspection, and on April 9, 1912- when this Government was in power-Mr. Pereira repeated the order for inspection, and said that Fraser was pressing for an 'answer. On April 15, 1912, Charles Grayson, a homestead inspector, recommended withdrawal; and on May 10, 1912, Pereira writes Fraser, the latest applicant, that the land when withdrawn would be sold 'by .auction. On November 16, 1912, F. Nelson, for the department, writes the Dominion Lands agent at 'Calgary ordering an inspection for valuation. On December 26, 1912, Inspector W. Tempany reports that the land is worth $5 an acre. On February 19, 1913, Mr. N. 0. Cote writes Fraser giving authority to purchase at $5 an acre; one-tquarter down, balance in three equal annual instalments. That is a case, if the value of the land were the same, on all fours with the Donaldson homestead. The land was under reservation. The practice of the department, and the regulations, require that whenever land is withdrawn from the reservation it should be offered for sale at public auction the reason being obvious. If the land is under reservation nobody has the opportunity to acquire it; when it is withdrawn, everybody should have an equal opportunity to acquire it. However, Fraser was able to make interest with the department just as Mr. Donaldson was, and the land was withdrawn and sold to him at a valuation. His neighbours were just as much entitled to the opportunity of acquiring this land as he was, but they were cut out from that opportunity, and, as I say, that is altogether contrary to the former practice of the department and is an entirely improper practice. A similar instance occurred in the town of GCmli on lake Winnipeg. A piece of land was under reservation there for many years, and finally-I think it was within the past year-it was withdrawn .and sold at a valuation to the then mayor of the town. It is useless to suggest that this is done in a fair spirit, or that it is giving every one a fait chance. It is just a matter of political favouritism. When the idea of political favouritism dominates the administration of the department a condition is created that is detrimental to the well-being of the settler of the western country and of all Canada.

The hon. gentleman, who has been a Minister of the Crown himself, knows how unusual it is to bring up oases of this nature when a Bill is before the House. It is impossible for any minister to have his memory charged with all the Information in reference to these cases of which he gets no notice whatever. He knows that it has been the practice, when Estimates are up, to bring up anything of this nature and discuss it and he also knows that it has not been the practice to bring up these matters on a public Bill which is engaging the attention of the House. I am quite well aware of the fact that stock-watering reserves, when they are withdrawn, when they are no longer required for stock-watering purposes, are offered for sale at auction. There is no regulation to that effect but that has been the practice and, I may say, a practice which was departed from by the hon. gentleman himself when he was the minister. One or two oases were presented to me during the hon. gentleman's administration in which he departed from that practice. I do not know -about these cases to which he has called my attention. 1 could not say from recollection whether they have been brought to my notice or not. Very likely they were disposed of by the department, as other cases are disposed of. I do not know whether they occurred while I was minister, but I cannot be expected to have my memory charged with the details of everything that has taken place in a vast department like the Department of the Interior. I shall be glad to inform myself on this subject and give all the information possible at the proper time.

I was not bringing the question before the House for the purpose of obtaining a reconsideration of the matter. I made a broad, general statement in regard to the administration of the Act and I thought it due to the House and to the minister that I should give absolute evidence of the facts as I stated them. I am not bringing it up for the purpose of getting a readjustment. I am bringing it up to establish the point that the administration is an administration of political favouritism and not an administration in the interests of the settler or the people.
If the hon. gentleman has been so guilty himself such a statement surely comes with bad grace from him.

I was minister for a number of years. My hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) was in opposition during those years, and any transgressions of -mine were sure-ly open for the consideration of the House at that time and are open yet if it is thought worth while to take up the time of the House in considering them. I laid down a definite principle when I was administering the affairs of the department, and I laid it down in print, made it absolutely public, and if I transgress from that I will have to take the responsibility and discredit of it. When I was administering the affairs of the department, and until I ceased to administer the affairs of the department, the records and results show that the people concerned were satisfied. They must have been satisfied or there would not have been the enormous amount of settlement which took place. Just as soon as the Government and system of administration changed the progress of settlement was checked. It is not an act of Providence, it is not a matter of chance, it is an actual and necessary result* of the change in method of administration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall section 1 be
adopted?

I wish to point out to the minister that section I as it is now drawn, is not in a shape that conveys to the ordinary man its intent and meaning. Instead of setting out on the face of the section what it is intended to mean, reference is made to two other sections further on in the Act. That confuses the mind of the ordinary individual and if it is desirable to amend the section, I wouid certainly urge that the amendment be made on the face of the section so that when a person who is interested in homesteading took up the law and read the section he would know everything that it was intended to convey, and he would not be obliged to refer to some other part of the Act and read some other sections to find out exactly what his rights were.

This section is intended to make the provision more clear in regard to the lands that will >be open for homesteading and the lands that will not be open. The references are to section 35 and 36. Section 35, which is a portion of the Act, refers to land adjacent to water-powers. Section 36 refers to land reserved for purposes of a harbour, landing, bridges, railway terminus, station or town site. It extends as well to all lands that are on the reserve list for any

purpose whatever. The Bill has been drafted by the law clerk of the House of Commons. I am not a lawyer myself, and not accustomed to the drafting of statutes, but I cannot see anything in the drafting of this Bill that would create any complication such as the hon. gentleman refers to.

I am not at all saying that the section as drafted is not perfectly good law, and I am not saying that a, member of the legal fraternity will not thoroughly understand it, but I do say that the ordinary citizen will not understand it as well as if the whole case were stated in the body of the section. That seems elementary.

Would not the whole
statute have to be re-enacted in order to do that?
No.
It would have to be consolidated and the whole reprinted and reenacted.

If it is desired to exempt from homestead entry lands adjacent to water-powers and lands reserved for other purposes you might as well state that in so many words in the section instead of having to refer to two other sections.
Where there is an addition to the law by the passage of a new Bill it is not customary to repeat what is contained in the original statute.

The section was drafted in order that it might be concise and at the same time explicit. It is a part of the one Act and all a person has to do, after he reads the first section, is to turn to sections 35 and 36 and they will show clearly the land to which homesteading is not applicable. It would mean the repetition of these very same sections in this section if it were drawn otherwise.

It is not for me to take the responsibility of drafting the section, but I did not think it right to let it pass without giving my opinion as a layman desiring to pass legislation which can be understood by other laymen.	-
Another point is that when we are declaring that lands contiguous to water-powers, and to certain other waters are reserved from settlement, who is to tell the prospective settler that this land is so reserved. Is he to be the judge of whether there is a possible water privilege at that place or not, or is it intended that if a man settles on such property his homestead

rights shall cease to exist because it is afterwards discovered that land is appurtenant to a water-power.
It would be only sensible to suppose that under such conditions he would have the privilege of locating somewhere else, and that has been the custom in the past.

But as the legislation is
now worded, that man is left without security for his outlay and the time he has expended.

It is assumed that the
Government will know what water-powers there are and that the Government will reserve whatever land they think proper in connection with that water-power, so that it will not be available for homestead entry.
If that were so stated in the Bill it would be all right, because the man would not get entry, but as it stands he is liable to get entry upon land which this Bill says he shall not hold.

The hon. gentleman knows that cases have arisen during his administration where settlers had to be removed from certain tracts that were reserved, and without any specific law these settlers were allowed to pick out the best land they could find elsewhere and all their homestead duties were allowed. That has been the custom from time immemorial, and the hon. gentleman himself has given effect to it when he was minister.
And I know how unfortunate it was to have to do it in some cases.
It did not hurt any one; they were as a rule better off.

In certain conditions a
very difficult situation has existed, and it is unfortunate that in amend-9 p.m. ment to the Act we should create such a condition as that of a settler who has located inside of a forest reserve.
In the case of the Winnipeg river we have made such a reservation as the hon. gentleman suggests. Any person who goes on land can see a waterpower, and he makes his entry at his own risk.

I am putting in my protest, and I do not wish to press the point. There are cases in which power can be created by a moderate expenditure of money, where there is no evidence to the
ordinary man in the natural condition that water-power exists. On the Bow river, application has been made to create a water-power at a certain place where there is a swift current, ibut no waterfall, and an ordinary settler would not be warned that a water-power existed there.

The point which my
hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) has raised exists in connection with timber reserves. I know a case in my own constituency in which a man has made entry for a homestead on land which was formerly a timber reserve, and having performed the work of clearing and expended nearly $5,000, he is now notified that he cannot get entry. This man thought he was in a district which was not of commercial value as a timber reserve.
How much timber did he take?
He took none; the timber was not of any commercial value, and he was preparing to burn it to get the land cleared.

What authority had
be to go on the land?

Other people had been getting entry in the same district. I must say in fairness to the minister that I have taken the matter up with him and he is prepared to deal with the case in a fair and equitable manner, but there is something wrong in a regulation which allows such a thing to occur. If we can remedy it in this case we should do so now when we are passing the legislation. We have in northern Alberta a lot of timber which is not of a merchantable character, and yet there may be more than the necessary twenty-five acres on a quarter-section to render it not available for settlement. The timber may be only fit for firewood, and on account of the distance from a railway it is of no value even as firewood, and the entrant would be delighted if a prairie fire swept it away, but yet this land is not eligible for entry. This regulation has had the effect of keeping a very considerable quantity of valuable land from being settled. I do not know that this particular case comes under section 2 of this Bill, but the question is worthy of consideration if in many cases timber lands, which have been reserved for timber purposes and which now prove to be of no value for merchantable timber, should not be thrown open and

the privilege given to settlers to make entry-on these lands without any drawbacks by the department.
The difficulty in the case to which my hon. Mend refers is that the man who made his entry swore that there was not more than twenty-five acres of timber.
Of merchantable timber.

If a man wilfully does that, you can see the difficulty which the department would experience in granting] entry. I believe, however, it is the practice of the department not to dispossess a man who has gone in and taken up land on which there is moire than twenty-five acres of timber; but he is asked to map out the twenty-five acres, and then the department issues permits to the settlers to cut on the balance of the land.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-proviso as to residence of entrant.

The whole question of [DOT] pre-emptions is re-opened in. this section. In the session of 1906-07, a Bill providing for pre-emptions was introduced by the present member far Edmonton, them Minister of the Interior of the late Government. His Bill was opposed partly by the late Hon. Thomas Greenway; and long speeches of criticism were made by hon. gentlemen opposite, notably by my hon. friend the present Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) and by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mir. Foster). The present Minister of the Interior by no means supported that legislation at that time and he allied himself with the late Mr. Greenway. If the minister desires a reference for that, I can give the same to him, although I suppose he recalls the statements he made at that time. He made certain objections to the way in which the regulation would work out, and on the whole he threw cold water on the scheme. The hon. member for North Toronto discouraged the proposition as much as possible, and said that the giving of this land was like the giving of money. On March 14, 1907, he spoke in this House as follows:
Your agriculturist is just as good a unit of the population and just as good a citizen of Canada, in Ontario, as he is in Saskatchewan or Manitoba. And one of his assets is his

share in the public franchises and the public property of this country. Yet, you propose to go to the treasury, and to take out of it millions of dollars, out of which you give him no benefit at all and you give it only to a section of. his class, a favoured few (so far as this goes) who reside within a certain area in the country. If those lands that you propose to give as largess, as bonus, to people who are outside of the area of need, not weighed down by poverty, not encountering difficulties, but so peaceful and happy and prosperous in the enjoyment of a princely gift of 160 acres of good land-if those lands which you propose to give them were transmuted into money, and that money were put into the treasury of this Dominion, it would he just exactly what it is now, though in a transmuted form. The transmutation of it - does not change its essential character, does not make it any less an asset of this country, in which every citizen has his share; and what do you propose to do? You propose to legislate out of the grand treasury of this country, for a few people in one section of it, millions of dollars of value, making them a present of that, and giving to none of the rest of the people of this country any share in the usufruct.
It was impossible to get the Bill through during that session on account of the opposition it met, and accordingly the Bill was introduced the following session in a slightly modified form and became law. The pre-emptions were very popular. My own district is the one in which by far the most pre-emptions have been taken up. On the first ^ of September, 1908, the pre-emption privilege was extended, .and everybody knows that it was the most popular thing in Canada at that time. Wherever preemptions and purchase homesteads were available, there was the greatest activity on the part of the people concerned to get the quarter-sections of their choice. The people were then satisfied-indeed they were grateful for the terms which the present member for Edmonton, then Minister of the Interior, granted to them. At that time there was prosperity throughout the West and there was no need for reducing the requirements and asking the people to dispense with the payment of the interest or with the residence duties. Unfortunately for our country that condition of prosperity has ceased. My bony friend to-day is graippling with a condition of affairs, which his own Government has created, in which the people require some relief. My hon. friend and his friends did what they could to keep from the people the relief offered to them in 1911 in the way of wider markets, and now it is necesisary for them to come to the people, in this condition that is more or less desperate with some measure of relief. The relief is brought in this form and I support it. In fact, there is no relief which I will not support in the

present condition of the people. The last tariff changes brought down have convinced me more than , ever that it is my duty to grasp and to encourage any measure of relief that this Government will give. For my part I will support the waiving of the payment altogether in order to give the people an opportunity, in the untoward circumstances and unfavourable environment in which they are now situated, to make a success. The minister is to be pitied more or less on account of the depression which has followed the existence of this Government just as surely as the night the day; but he must realize in his heart that, if the people who grow their wheat and other cereals on their homesteads and pre-emptions had the open market at their door, the three years' interest of $72 would be a mere bagatelle to them, and the minister would not have had this cry from them.
The minister in one way is inconsistent in this Bill. If I understand him correctly-I am speaking not of the interest part, but of the residence part-it is his intention that, after a man has completed his residence duties, if he has $480, Tie can get patent for his pre-emption if he has fifty acres of breaking done; but if he has not $480 that year but has it the next year, then when he conies a year or two years later, as the case may be, he is not forgiven his residence duties in the interval.
Am I right in saying that a man who has spent two years after the protection time commences in working and slaving under unfavourable circumstances to get the $480, is charged up, after he gets that amount, with eighteen months' residence?
That is right.

I want to protest
against that. It seems that even in respect of this small amount the Government is discriminating in favour of the man who has the ready money as against the man who has to worir hard to raise the amount. It seems 'to me that that is unjust discrimination. I have constituents who can pay the $480 at once, but I have a great many more who cannot. Unfortunately, under the present Government, the latter class is becoming larger and the former class is becoming smaller. I protest against making these people comply with the residence required because ' they are compelled to wait a little while to earn the money. I cannot conceive why the richer man should be forgiven; why he should be relieved of his residence duties for six months,, in the year while the poor man has
to work and slave for it, perhaps keeping a wife and family at the same time. I ask the minister to adjust this matter; I ask him to do what is right by the man in poorer circumstances. I ask in the name of many thousands of my constituents that he afford to the poorer man the same relief from residence duties that he grants to the richer man.

If the homesteader chooses to avail himself of the provisions of the present Act as it is now upon the statute books he will he in no worse position in the future than he is at the present time, and he will be in a better position in that he will have to pay no interest during the first three years. He has the option of taking the time provided by the present statute in order to get the patent for his pre-emption, or of taking advantage of one of the provisions of this Bill: that at the end of three years, when he secures the patent for his homestead, he may, by paying his pre-emption money, secure a patent for his pre-emption. He is thus relieved of his homestead duties in the future, provided he has put in the necessary residence up to that time and performed the necessary cultivation duties. It is not a question of discrimination as between the rich man and the poor man; many poor men have asked for a provision of this kind. If a man has the ready money, he can cultivate or improve his preemption, if he so desires. This provision is intended to give all the option of continuing under the present Act and to improve their position to the extent of forgiving them their interest. Or, if they deBire, by raising money on their homestead, to get a patent, at the end of the time they qualify for homestead they may qualify for patent for pre-emption by making the necessary payment. The hon. gentleman has placed a rather strained interpretation upon this Act as at present drafted, it is not designed at all to discriminate in favour of the rich man.

I would remind the committee that the area of land that this section refers to is that portion which, roughly speaking, begins east of the centre of the southern boundary of the province, runs north westerly and northerly along the third meridian up to the forty-fourth township and thence westerly and southerly and easterly to the place of commencement. The inhabitants of that area were given the special privilege of taking up homestead and purchasing pre-emption
I am sorry the minister cannot accede to my request in the matter of residence duties. His answer, however, must be final.

The minister must recognize that he is making a very important departure in our land regulations by his amendment in section 2. I have always

understood that the purpose of having this duty demanded from entrants for homesteads and for purchase homesteads was to have the land actually brought under cultivation, and not to give our land a speculative value that might be given to it by the spending of a few dollars in cultivation without having the entrants perform a certain amount of residence on the land.
I am hot going to say whether the minister is right or wrong, the hon. member for Moosejaw has given reasons why conditions could be made more lenient in these days than they have been in days gone by, but I would say to the minister, notwithstanding his explanations, and I tried to follow them as closely as possible, that I am still afraid he is doing an injustice to a great many entrants for pre-emptions throughout the West. He makes the statement that by giving the privilege of paying $480, the price of a pre-emption homestead, he is actually lessening the onerous conditions of the pre-emption. I fail to see that. The real effect is that the minister is compelling the man who cannot furnish the money to go on and perform residence duty; and he cannot fail to see that he is putting a premium on the case where a man can take out from his bank account $480 and free himself from all future responsibility. It may be urged that the man who has not the means can go to the bank when the bank knows that he is going to get his patent for pre-emption shortly, and get the money to pay off the Government. But what kind of bargain would that be for the man who has not the means to make the payment? The Government charge him five per cent, but the bank would probably charge him ten per cent or twelve per cent. I should assume the minister is penalizing that man who wants to get his patent by going to the bank or the trust company or the mortgage or loan company from five per cent to seven per cent, if he wants to have the same privilege as the man who has the money in the bank and who can make the payment to the Government. The minister cannot get away from that. The minister is taking the responsibility of making the conditions of life less onerous for certain of the settlers who have had the privilege of taking purchase homesteads or pre-empted homesteads. If he is going to change those conditions, he ought to make the conditions equal to all parties concerned. Why should the minister penalize this man? Here are both cases, the man who can pay up at the end of three years from the date of his
homestead entry, and the man who cannot. Both of these parties, under the legislation now proposed, will be exempted from three years interest. After three years from the time at which the entry was made for the homestead you find the conditions exactly the same so far as these men are concerned, they both have three years' exemption from interest.
The conditions are absolutely even up to that point, but then they become absolutely different. The man who can pay down $480 jash is to be relieved of all further responsibility as to residing on his pre-empted homestead, while the man who cannot afford to pay the $480-unless he borrows it and pays 10 per cent or 12 per cent interesG-is to be penalized by having to perform still further residence duties. I do not think that is a square deal. If the minister wants to do something to make himself popular with the homesteaders,-and Lord knows he needs it, at any rate this Government at Ottawa do-if he is going to make conditions of life less onerous for the men who have purchased pre-emptions in that particular area he should make the conditions absolutely even, and no amount of argument can persuade me that conditions contained in section 2 of this Bill are in any way just and right as between the man who has means and the man who has not.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-price:

The minister seems unwilling to assist us in the matter of readjusting the residence duties on pre-emptions, but perhaps he will meet us on this. The minister lays it down as correct-and I think it is wise legislation at this juncture -that the entrant shall not pay interest on his $480 for the first three years after he enters on his pre-emption. He must pay it after the pre-emption time, so to call it, commences to run. I am not quite sure how the minister is going to ruin this thing. His Bill looks to me to be a very strange one. We have just passed clause 2, and I am quite sure no man in the House can tell us just what it means. For instance, it says you will have to do the residence duties for the fraction of time during which you are rustling for the $480. But if it takes a man fifteen months to get that amount, how much residence duties would he have to do? But the minister, following his practice of doing no wrong, will no doubt see that it is carried out correctly. The department will have some trouble over that; it is ill-digested. The responsibility, however, is

on the minister who does not seem to care to discuss it with us. Perhaps he will tell us later how much residence duty the man will have to do who has to go out and rustle fifteen months to get the $480. With regard to section 3 a strange principle is involved. For the first three years the man is charged no rent and no interest. At the end of the third year, or whenever his pre-emption time commences, he pays down a dollar an acre and commences to pay interest on the $320. Why should he pay interest on the $320 more than on the $480? It cannot be for rent, because he has had the use of the land all the time, and it cannot be to show the earnestness of his bargain, because he has already paid $160. If he should be forgiven his interest for the first three years, he should be forgiven every cent the Government can take off his back; he should be forgiven all the interest. If he is not to be charged interest on the $480, he should not be charged interest on the balance of $320. The minister says he will commence to use the land more after the third year; but he has had the use of the land from the start and can grow as good a crop in the second year as in the fifth or sixth. I think the minister should make this interest-waiving apply to the whole amount. I wish to move the following amendment:
That section 3 be amended by striking out all the words between the word ' instalments ' in the eighth line of said section and the word ' provided ' in the fourteenth line thereof and substituting the following:
Any instalment or instalments not paid on the due date'thereof shall bear interest at the rate of five per centum per annum from such due date until the date of payment, but no Instalment shall bear interest prior to the due date thereof.
I hope the minister will agree to that.

I think the hon. member for Moosejaw is using the wrong term when he states that the man is being penalized because he has to pay interest after the expiration of the first three years. Is he penalized at the present day. The only way he is being penalized under this Act is that he is being forgiven the first three years' interest, and if that is penalizing, I think the pre-emptor will be very glad to be penalized in that manner. The interest starts under this Act at the end of the first three years on the $480. If the pre-emptor should pay an instalment of $100, or Whatever it may be, he will have to pay interest on just that much less; so he is not being

penalized at all. I do not think there is any necessity for the hon. gentleman's amendment, though I am quite willing that the section should stand for further consideration and amendment. Both the hon. member for Moosejaw and the hon. member for Humboldt have said that we are penalizing the poor man.

We will cut out the
word penalizing, and say charging. Penalizing may be a little strong, but I feel very keenly about this matter.

It is an impossibility not
to have inequalities so long as there is an unequal distribution of wealth. I do not think it is necessary to charge the present Act with undue discrimination against the poor man, for I have brought this amendment in largely at the instance of the poor pre-emptor who desires to secure his homestead patent in order that he may raise the money, to pay for his pre-emption at the same time. I am sure that they will not feel they are being discriminated against simply because the rich man may be able to pay at the end of the three years. The poor man has exactly the same option. He an pay at the end of the three years, or go on paying exactly as under the present Act. The hon. gentleman's argument, as I understand it, is that the poor homesteader is being discriminated against. I am lightening his burdens by taking off three years' interest, and he has the option of getting his homestead patent and raising the money to pay for his pre-emption at the same time, or he can go on paying for it as the present Act provides.

I do not think the minister quite understands me. I do not say that John Smith is any worse off because you are good to George Brown; but it is not fair to be good to George Brown and not apply the same principle to John Smith. John Smith may have to wait two years before he gets his money and he has to do twelve months' residence duties. Suppose the minister made a law that he would not charge $3 an acre to men whose names commence with the letters A to M, and that he would charge the full price to the other fellows whose names start with the letters N to Z; to the men whose names begin with the letters from N to Z the minister says:	Although I have
not charged these other people, I shall charge you, but you are not hurt as you are the same as you were. Perhaps penalizing would not be the word to use, but there

would be discrimination. The minister has not answered the point that there is an unfair discrimination in his proposed legislation against a man who has to wait a year before he gets his $420 gathered together as compared with the man who happens to have the money in the bank.
Do I understand the minister to say that he is going to let that section stand?
I would not like to accept the amendment without giving it further consideration.
Have there been any preemptions granted under the Act of 1908?
Yes.
I notice that the minister, according to his footnote, is going to make this measure retroactive as far as present entrants for pre-emption are concerned? Is that not the purport of the measure?
We are going to allow any person who has not qualified, that is, who has not obtained his patent up to the present time, to come under the provisions of the Act.

The man who may have
held his entry for five or six years, but who has not complied with these regulations and has not obtained his patent, is going to get the benefit of a certain number of years' interest. What about the man who has in the last year or so applied for and obtained his patent, should the minister not give his case consideration? He has his patent, it is true, but he has obtained it under the conditions that he had to pay and perform the residence duties.
