Surely, because one man has been a little slower than another in applying for his patent, the minister is not going to penalize the man who has been good enough to promptly pay the Government what is due and to fulfil his residence and other duties?

Now the hon. gentleman is putting up an argument for the man who has money and has been fortunate and wealthy enough to pay for his pre-emption. There were 879 patents issued for preemption. What would this amount to? If we were to refund to these 879 people it would amount to a little over $2,000,000. If I were to bring down a Supplementary Estimate for $2,000,000 to refund to those who have paid for the right of pre-emption, would the hon. gentleman support such a proposition as that?
Has the minister actually figured up that the interest charges on patents already granted would amount to over $2,000,000?	.

No, not the interest
charges.
I am speaking of the interest charges. The minister is not proposing to pay back the principal?

I was referring to principal and interest.
Section stands.
On section 4-entrant not required to erect house on purchased homestead:

Under clause 4 a question may arise which .affects particularly the northern part of the province of Alberta. We are exempted from the provisions of this pre-emption act inasmuch as no pre-emptions are allowed north of the 44th township. I think this is working a hardship because the northern section of Alberta is. largely a brush country and a homesteader m.ay not have arable land enough on his quarter-section of 160 acres to permit him to earn a livelihood. This makes it necessary that he should be enabled to secure more land. I think that the minister should grant, in lieu of pre-emption privileges being allowed in the northern part of Alberta, the Tight to homesteaders or entrants to take up purchased homesteads ini that section of the province. We have in the Peace river country a tremendous amount of arable land and we also have a large number of people who have acquired homesteads possibly in other provinces or who have exhausted their homestead rights either by abandonment or in some other manner and I think it .should be the policy of the department to allow these people to have the privilege of acquiring a purchased homestead such as is granted in the province of Saskatchewan, and in the southern part of Alberta, under the purchased homestead provisions. In the northern section of Alberta the purchased homestead area should be extended so as to permit entrants to obtain purchased homesteads. If the minister will not acquiesce in this suggestion I would like to move	-
That section 28 he amended by striking out the words 'open for entry in the manner set forth in this section ' when they occur in lines 22 and 23 thereof, and by further striking out

all the words contained in lines 36 to 53 thereof, both inclusive.
This is to permit of purchased homesteads being acquired north of township 44.

Purchased homesteads

A good many homesteads in northern Saskatchewan are covered with brush and timber. The land is arable, but it costs a good deal to clear it. The hon. member for Strathcona states that it costs from $22 to $25 an acre to clear the land around Edmonton, and the same conditions exists in northern Saskatchewan. In some homesteads the land is very fertile, but is covered with brush and other timber, -and it costs in some cases as high as $30 to clear the land. Consequently the farmer in the northern portion of the province is handicapped to a great extent as compared with the farmer on the prairie. We have already dealt with the privilege the farmer on the prairie has of taking a free homestead and purchasing pre-emption, and, in addition to that, with the land on his homestead, the very day he lands there he can put his team of horses or his traction engine on his ploughs and start ploughing the whole 160 acres. ing perhaps $15, $20 and as high as $30 an acre. What is the interpretation to be put upon the words ' arable land? That is just what we want to obviate in northern Saskatchewan. We want to have the privilege that where a homesteader cannot find the required number of acres clear of timber and brush to prove up for his homestead he should be allowed, instead of cultivating that homestead, to prove up by the cattle. Under this Act the homesteader, before he can secure his patent, has to fence his land although not actually necessary for practical purposes. I submit that that clause should be changed so as to make it possible for the homesteader to get his patent without necessarily having to fence his land.

I wish to endorse what the hon. member for Prince Albert has said in regard to scrub land. In the section from which I come three-fourths of the homesteads are composed of scrub land, which costs the settler from $15 to $30 an acre to clear. No more than at the
present time in connection with homesteads.

scrub land which was absolutely useless as regards the commercial value of its timber or scrub. The question is a large one, and I do not know how you can regulate the matter, but I think there should be some recourse from the report of the homestead inspector in case he puts in a biased report, because I know of many cases in' which homesteaders have been discriminated against by the homestead inspector, not from political motives, but as a matter of judgment as to what constitutes arable land. What , the hon. member for Prince Albert has said with regard to the cost of clearing scrub land is absolutely true. It is a very expensive operation, and I am glad to hear that in some cases the minister requires only six acres cleared instead of thirty, because to clear six acres of scrub land represents more cash outlay than to clear thirty acres of prairie land. Many farmers are loth to enter upon scrub land, and I think the more latitude the department allows entrants on that class of land the better it will be for the settlement of the country. I reiterate that in northern Alberta three-fourths of the land available for homesteads is scrub land, which entails a tremendous expense to clear; and any alleviation the department can give to those homesteaders is absolutely in the interest of the country at large. I do not want this section to pass without emphasizing to some extent what has been said by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. When a homesteader applies for patent at the end of three years' residence, or four or five, as the case may be, I do not think it should be left to the homestead inspector at that stage of the proceedings-I do not care whether he has had the power in the

(past or not-to decide whether or not that homesteader has fulfilled the requirements of the Act as to keeping so many head of stock, or breaking so many acres of land. A homestead inspector should not have that authority. It gives the homestead inspector the power to make it difficult or easy for the applicant as his sympathies may dictate in each instance. The minister has increased the staff very considerably, he has spent a lot of money on that department of the public service and consequently he will not tell us that these men are overburdened with work. If the declaration of the applicant shows that the land is inclined to be rough in character, heavily wooded, and that sort of thing, the beginning of the residence of the homesteader is the proper time to have the inspection and declaration made so that this homesteader may then take his choice .as to whether he will carry out his duties by cultivation of a certain area of land or take advantage of the stock provision. One man of our company named Neil McKay, now of New Brunswick, got paid last fall. His claim is no better than mine. There are very few of the number living now.
There are other parts of the letter that do not relate to this matter which I need not read. Here is a letter addressed to me from a man named N. E. Mathewson:
Seeing that you have interested yourself in provincial volunteers and their pay at the time of the Fenian raid, I take the liberty of sending you the enclosed sketch of the Strathal-byn volunteers at the time. I suppose it is too late for any of us who are yet living to look for any recognition.
This is the sketch that he sent:
At the first murmur of danger the young men of Strathalbyn formed themselves into a volunteer company and called themselves the Strathalbyn volunteers. They elected me as their captain, the late Mr. A. B. McKenzie, lieutenant and Mr. Alexander Stewart, ensign. They assembled regularly for drill. I was their instructor, for there was no other convenient, and I had studied the manual then in use, and when we received our rifles, I taught them the manual of arms, and superintended their rifle practice. For some time we were drilled by a sergeant from H.M.O. 16th regiment, then stationed at Halifax. Lieutenant Governor George Dundas, at that time Commander-in-Chief of our island came out to see the company and was pleased with it. A squad of my company camped at the annual shooting match in Charlottetown.
This is a letter from a Mr. Keefe, dated February 18 last:
I drilled at the time Of the Fenian raid. The captain of the company I drilled in was Law-
rence Peters. Malcolm Leslie was drill sergeant assisted by a drill sergeant from Halifax. Our ages were taken and our height, also sworn in. We were liable to a fine of $25 if we were not in the ranks. We drilled in Souris and Rollo Bay. That would be in lot 44. I was living in Rollo Bay at that time.
Here is a letter from a man now living in Gloucester, Massachusetts:
I have been informed that all the men that served In the militia at the time of the Fenian raid in 1864 and 1865 have been awarded $100 by the Canadian Government. I have been speaking to five or six who have received their money. Now, I drilled for two years at Souris, Rollo Bay and the North Side, East point. I do not just rerqember our captain's name, hut our adjutant's name was Leslie, and our covering sergeant was John McIntyre. As I was born in Souris, I wrote to James Mineghy, but could not get any information concerning the bounty.
Here is a letter from a man named Peter Gormley, who appeared to be active in the service at the time. He gives a list of the men who drilled with him and who went about thirty miles from their homes for that purpose. His letter, which is addressed to myself, reads as follows:
Having read in the paper of the inquiry of volunteers at the time of the Fenian raid of 1866, I will give you a list of some of them. I am informed by those who served or drilled for two years or more, and I was present at every call. The last was at South Port, Prince Edward Island. Every one had to find himself and no pay for their time. Each one had to board or find himself in his eatables. I will give you a list of the people on St. Mary's road.
Here is the list:
Dan. Hughes, Michael Gormley, James Gormley, James McGuigan, Patrick McGuigan, John McGuigan, Thomas McCarron, Dan. McKenna, Thomas Hughes, Bernard McGuigan, Brian McCarron, Thomas Cassidy, Martin McCarthy, William McCarthy, Robert McCarron, Patrick McGee, Alex. Lawson, John Lavertv, Colin Steel, Donald R. Steele, Patrick Mckearney, Thomas Daly, John McCarron.
I think that if any men in the Dominion of Canada are entitled to recompense for what they did on that occasion, these men are. The Legislature of the province did everything that was necessary. Members of the Legislature at that time said that they were willing that the Prince Edward Island volunteers should go to the other provinces if they could render better assistance in that way than by remaining on the island. I think they did as much as was done by any other province. While the volunteers were not technically called out by proclamation, everything was done that could be done; the procedure was just as complete as if the volunteers had been

called out by Governor's proclamation. I would ask the minister not to insist upon the words ' called out by proclamation.'

I think the minister's amendment would not be of any advantage to my hon. friend the hon. member for Kings, Prince Edward Island, because the resolution would apply only in cases where the volunteers had been called out by proclamation of the Governor in Council. I understood my hon. friend to say that while there was no technical proclamation by the Government, there was action by the Legislature which would be substantially the same thing. I assume also from what he said that there was voluntary drilling of volunteers, although there was no regular militia at that time other than that which was initiated under the Art passed that year.

Section 2 of the Act passed in 1912 reads as follows.
In this Act 'volunteer' means any person who was regularly enrolled or enlisted m and served with any militia corps which the Government of Canada, or of Nova Scotia, or ot New Brunswick called out for active service m the year one thousand eight hundred and sixty-six or which the Government of Canada called out for active service in the year one thousand eight hundred and seventy, excepting, however, the two battalions of riflemen formed for active service in the Northwest.
As was stated by the hon. member for Kings the Legislature of Prince Edward Island provided for this emergency. The ninth clause of the Government's speech was as follows:
It is with feelings of just pride that we have observed the loyalty and spirit evinced by our fellow citizens in the neighbouring provinces when threatened by piratical attacks at the hands of lawless men.
Mr, MACDONALD:	Does it specifically
mention the Fenians?

The Fenians were the only men who were disturbing the peace of the country' at that time. A unanimous vote of the Legislature of Prince Edward Island was passed pledging the whole revenue and resources of the island towards rendering assistance to repel this attack, and at the same session a militia Act was passed. That militia Act was sent to England for the assent of the Queen. Some objection was taken to it by the Colonial Secretary and it was returned with the suggestion that it be re-enacted. In the session ol 1866 the Aot was repassed with amendments. In the meantime, in the month of January, 1865, all the militia was called
out; if you look at the journals of the House of Assembly of Prince Edward Island you will find the Adjutant General's report of the militia of the province. It was an unusual thing to call the militia out at this time; the purpose was that Prince Edward Island should be in the *same position as the other provinces so far as repelling the piratical attacks referred to in the Governor's address was concerned. In the year 1865 large sums of money were voted to equip the militia and at the inspection of the militia in the city of Charlottetown in 1865 there were present
1,000	men. That was not an ordinary thing in the province of Prince Edward Island at that time. Of these men, 813 were equipped with uniforms. In the meantime the British Government had loaned the colony a large number of rifles; the Adjutant General's report states where these rifles were and how they were being used. The journals of the House of Assembly of: that year show that a large sum of money was expended for the purpose of organizing the militia and of putting them in shape in order that they might go into the field if necessary. So we have the militia of Prince Edward Island in the same position as the militia of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Canada. It is true that they were not called out by special order of the Governor of the province of Prince Edward Island, but the Legislature of the province made the provision that they should be put into a position to go into the field if necessary. As will be found in the Adjutant General's report, a number of drills were held; the number of officers and men and the quantity of equipment are also mentioned. Full details may be- found in the journals of the Assembly of Prince Edward Island. I understand that all these men were properly enrolled, and that the enrolment lists are to-day in the city of Halifax. When the militia was taken away from Charlottetown six or seven years ago, the militia authorities in Halifax asked that all papers in connection with the militia of Prince Edward Island should be handed over to the Dominion authorities. Without any reference to the authorities in Prince Edward Island, all of the old militia lists were handed over and sent on to Halifax. This was an improper proceeding on the part of Dominion authorities because these lists of the militia of Prince Edward Island before Confederation should have remained in the hands of the provincial authorities. They are to-day, however, in the hands of the authorities at Halifax and

if the minister would take the trouble he *could get them and see exactly What the condition of affairs was in 1866. I do not think the conditions in Prince Edward Island differed very much from the condition in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, and the militia of Prince Edward Island are entitled to the same considerations as the militia of Nova Scotia or of New Brunswick. If the technicality of the calling out of the militia is to be taken into consideration, and if the authorities in Ottawa insist that this proclamation must be produced, we cannot produce it, but I think that the technicality should not be allowed to be insisted upon in a matter of this kind. If the militia in Nova Scotia are paid, those in Prince Edward Island are as much entitled to it as they. It is true that a great sum has 'been paid to these men and the probability is that many people who are *entitled to this grant will not receive it. If the Dominion Government insists that the [DOT]authorities in each province shall produce the Order in Council, then, of course, the militia in Prince Edward Island cannot get the grant; but I do not think that would be a fair way to deal with the militia in Prince Edward Island, who did as much as the militia in any other province. Many of the militia in Nova Scotia and Upper Canada simply drilled, they were called out *and met at a certain place and were inspected by an officer and that is all that happened. They get their $100. Why should not those in Prince Edward Island get theirs? There is no reason. If the Government of Canada insists that that proclamation should be produced, then I would ask them to deal in a different way with the militia of Prince Edward Island, that is to grant the Government of Prince Edward Island a sum equivalent to the money which they spent in the calling out and drilling of the militia and a certain sum for the militia wlho were called out. There must be some way of dealing with this matter in order to do something for the militia of the different provinces who took part in the emergency.

I beg to submit an amendment. I think it will cover the ground and I am sure it will meet with the approval of the minister and of the committee:
That the resolution be amended by adding after the words * New Brunswick ' in the sixth line ' or who drilled in the province of Prince Edward Island In preparation for repelling the threatened Fenian invasion of 1886 and 1870.'

Mr. SAM. HUGHES:	I am sure the
House is very much interested and instructed by the data which have been placed before us by the two representatives of Prince Edward Island. It shows a splendid spirit in anticipation. But I think the hon. member for King's failed to note that in introducing the subject as he did, by quoting from the proceedings of the legislature of Prince Edward Island that they had observed with pride how the people of the neighbouring provinces had turned out to repel the threatened invasion, he made it evident that the threatened invasion had passed and gone before they were organized. The keynote of the whole matter is that if the militia were called out for active service in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Canada they complied with the law, and I am sure my hon. friends from Prince Edward Island would not ask for anything more than the other provinces receive. If they were called out for active service they come under the Act. If they were not called out for active service they do not come under the Act. Therefore, in consenting to insert the words * Prince Edward Island,' I think ample justice will be done to the people and representatives of that province. The amendment proposed by the hon. member for King's (Mr. J. J. Hughes) would simply hand over the bounty of $100 to every man between the ages of 16 and 60 in the province. There was not a part of the province of Ontario but turned out at that time to drill. In Nova Scotia there was undoubtedly a very peculiar condition of affairs. There was a universal compulsory service law in Nova Scotia, and the entire militia of that province were called out under that Act. It was a rather peculiar condition of affairs. Nevertheless they turned out, they were called out and I believe, from all the evidence submitted to the committee in the House here from representatives of both parties in the province, they turned out loyally and well on that occasion. If there is any evidence of that kind from Prince Edward Island, I would be glad to insert the words * Prince Edward Island,' but the amendment of the hon. member for King's of course would be ridiculous. . It would simply hand over the money to every man in Nova Scotia who was an adult at that time.

I do not like to harp
back and say, I told you so; but if the minister will remember that when the Bill was introduced in 1912 I called his attention to

-the fact that he would have a lot of difficulty in the administration of the law, because he did not properly describe what -was meant by the words ' called out.' If he will refer to the debate of that year he will find that I particularly called his attention to that fact. I do not pretend to have any more insight into these things than any other member, but from my little knowledge of militia matters I should say that a lot of the difficulty started from that. There were not over 600 in Nova Scotia, and yet he is compelled to stand up and tell us that the men were called out and loyally obeyed the summons. He does not believe that in his heart himself.
Oh, yes, he does.

No, he does not. He
knows that this is one of the most contemptible scandals in [DOT] Canadian history. Twelve thousand or fifteen thousand men have received $100 each in Nova Scotia who were never called out in the proper sense any more than I was called out, and I was only born a year $r two before that. It is true there was a proclamation by the Government of Nova Scotia calling out the active militia to perform annual drill, probably in anticipation of the Fenian raid. I daresay that they met the technical requirements of his Act. But does the minister believe that a man away down in Cape Breton island who was called out to perform annual drill really complied with the spirit of the Bill passed in 1912 providing a Fenian Raid bounty of $100? That is 48 years ago. Assuming that the man was eighteen years of age when he became a member of the active militia, that would make him 66 years of age to-day Does my hon. friend believe that there are
15.000	militia men in Nova Scotia to-day, 66 years of age, who were members of the militia at that time? It is not possible. I believe thousands of men in Nova Scotia have been paid who were barely born at the time of the Fenian Raid, and my hon. friend knows it. He believes it anyway. It is simply a scandal.

There is evidence that
81.000	men responded to the call at that time in Nova Scotia alone.

That is the evidence
now, I dare say, but go back 48 years ago and what was the evidence then? I think that nearly every able-bodied man in Nova Scotia claims now that he was a member of the militia at that time, and was called out. I was down in Nova Scotia when the
minister's officials were going around. In the first place there were two or three officials from Ottawa; then a provincial organizer came down to lead the Ottawa officials round; a county official then appeared, and he was drumming them up. They held meetings in each constituency.
I went down with my hon. friend from Guysborough to hold a political meeting,at Canso, and the whole crowd was on the same boat drumming up these veterans.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: Did the hon. member tell them on that occasion that they were all fakes?

No, I was not discussing that question at all, because I did not believe the minister was going to be fool enough to be caught by it. Perhaps if I had realized how easy the minister is I might have had something to say. They were only getting ready for the coup at that time. I know the minister is flighty, to use as mild a term as possible, when it comes to militia matters, and that he is not governed by the ordinary horse sense that actuates him in the business affairs of life. I think the minister would make every man a Colonel who would accept it, or a Brigadier-General. He would give away all the resources of Canada to militia men if his followers would allow him to do so. But the minister has sane business moments, and he knows that a great fraud is being perpetrated upon his department by the people of Nova Scotia. If he has a law which is capable of being so interpreted that frauds are being perpetrated upon the country why does not the minister amend his law to prevent this, and to bring within its purview those who are properly entitled to "the bounty? If it be necessary to bring in Prince Edward Island, bring it in, but on a reasonable business basis. Give these people a bounty if they are entitled to it, but if they are not, do not. I want to compliment the minister in that there has been no scandal in connection with this matter in my province. I think the minister has tried to administer the law fairly in most cases. I have two or three complaints before me, which I shall call to his attention later, but, generally speaking, I think the law has been fairly administered. I think the great majority of those entitled to the bounty have received it. In New Brunswick, there really was an attempted invasion of Canada. I think only three points in the whole Dominion were threatened. One was in western Ontario, another in the Eastern Townships, and the other

point was near St. Andrews, in New Brunswick. The people of New Brunswick responded, generally, and I think there was no outside assistance. They came from Woodstock, my own town, from Fredericton, and different points 100 miles away, and the threatened invasion was repelled. I think they only did their duty; they only did what British subjects ought to do, and what common humanity teaches every man to do-to defend his home and fireside. As I said before, I very much doubt the wisdom of the minister's granting a bounty at all. I do not see any reason why a man should be rewarded for defending his home and fireside in case of emergency. But if my hon. friend is determined-I think for political purposes-to grant this money, surely it ought to be granted in a sane business-like manner, and if he would apply the law all over Canada as in New Brunswick I do not think there would be much fault to find. I repeat that the manner in which these
15,000	people in Nova Scotia have been paid the bounty is simply a scandal. They never expected to be called out on active service; they never realized what it meant, and when the minister passed his law I do not think he realized what it meant. He used the words ' called out,' and it so happened that his friends in Nova Scotia found that the conditions fitted in with the words of the Act, and the minister had not the moral courage to repeal it. I have a few individual cases to bring to the attention of my hon. friend so that he can amend the law to meet these cases. On general principles I want to know if .the minister will not try to get down to real honest business, and if he feels he has a right to pass a law providing a bounty to do it in a way that will reflect credit upon his department?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the hon. member that the amendment before the committee provides for an enlargement of the provisions made in the resolution under consideration, and therefore I must rule the hon. member out of order.

The motion is before the committee as well as the amendment, and I think members are at liberty to discuss it. I supported this Act at its Inception, and I have not changed my mind since. I want to say a few words in response to my hon. friend the member .for Carleton 'Mr. Carvell). I think my hon. friend is altogether mistaken, and 
does not understand the facts as regards ,Nova Scotia at that time. Very great preparations were made in that province- much greater preparations, I have no doubt, than in any other province of Canada. For certain reasons the people of .Nova Scotia were very much alarmed at .the time. They expected an attack by sea, and the entire militia of the province was ordered out and turned out. There was a very strong force of militia in Nova .Scotia at the time, considering the population of the province. No man who reads the history of those days, and the discussions in the local legislature, and who makes himself acquainted with conditions in Nova Scotia at that time, will have any doubt of the fact that there was a very large force of militia prepared to take a hand against this invasion, if it had been necessary to do so; but, of course, everyone is well ^.ware that the real invasion never took place; and that, in the view of some people, is a weakness in the claims of those people for compensation. The title to compensation rests, I understand, on a legal p(?int: on the words of a proclamation which was issued on the 17th of March, 1866, which reads as follows:
Proclamation by His Excellency Sir William Fenwick Williams.
Whereas a hostile invasion of the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is threatened, by which the lives and property of Her Majesty's subjects therein may be put in jeopardy, and preparations are necessary to repel such invasion if made:
And, whereas, in such an emergency, I am by law authorized and required to call out the. militia force of Nova Scotia in aid of Her Majesty's regular forces for its defence:
I do hereby command and require all officers, non-commissioned officers, and privates of the militia force of Nova Scotia, and all persons liable to perform militia duty in said province, to turn out for actual service as in time of war, according to law, and subject, on failure so to do, to the pains, penalties, and forfeitures thereby imposed and provided.
Of which all persons interested will take notice, and govern themselves accordingly.
Given under my hand and seal at Halifax, this seventeenth day of March, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and sixty-six, and in the twenty-ninth year of Her Majesty's reign.
By command of His Excellency the Lieutenant Governor and Commander-in-chief.
Charles Tupper.
You will note that this proclamation, orders the whole force of Nova Scotia out for actual service as in time of war. The language happens to be the same as the language in the Act which we have passed and I suppose it was unknown to the minister at the time this proclamation existed in the form in which it does. There is ample

proof that the force responded very loyally to this call. Sir Charles Tupper was Premier of Nova Scotia and the legislature *met just about that time. On the 19th of March the Premier of the province laid this proclamation (before the members of the legislature and he made a statement which is contained in the following minute of the legislature:
Hon. Provincial Secretary laid on the table, by command of His Excellency the Lieutenant-Governor, a copy of the proclamation made by the Commander-in-Chief, calling: out the militia of the province, and in so doing moved the following resolution:
Resolved, that this House cordially approve of the action of His Excellency the Commander-in-Chief calling out the militia, as stated in the proclamation now laid on me table, and will provide for any expense required for the adequate protection of the province.
He said the condition of this province in relation to its local defence had occupied the attention of the Government and the Imperial authorities for a considerable period. It was of recent date, however, owing to circumstances to which he need not particularly allude, because they were familiar to every member

owing to the fact that a large body of lawless men were openly and publicly, in the heart of the adjoining republic, threatening the securities, the rights and liberties, of the people of British North America-that the subject had beeome one of immediate importance.
Mr. Prior said:
That the most cordial reception and the most hearty cheering had greeted the reading of the proclamation of His Excellency the Commander-in-Chief by the regiments who that day had been mustered on the common. He was confident that should the foe invade our province there would he hearts and hands to meet them on the threshold and to defend the hearth stones of our country. He gave this information not because the country would need any additional inducement hut in order that the slight and sarcasm that was frequently thrown upon a mixed population like that of Halifax might have no effect.
Sir Charles Tupper also made the following remarks:
Numbers of persons had been sent to Ireland, and large sums had been contributed to a movement having for its object the subversion of the integrity of the empire, by securing the independence of Ireland from British rule. While he believed that by proper precautions being taken we need not continue in apprehension, the Government had felt it their duty to watch most narrowly the course of affairs, and to take such measure as the security of the country might require. After the adjournment of the House on Saturday, information had been received of such character as to demand instantaneous action. Under the law, the only means by which the militia force could he made available for active service was by a proclamation embodying the militia, and placing them in a position in which their services could be readily
obtained. He was unwilling to place before the House the information that had been received by His Excellency and by the Commander-inChief of Her Majesty's forces, and the House would absolve him from any such necessity, because such a course would be extremely prejudicial to the public interests, as it would have the effect of cutting off the sources of information hitherto at command, and so far from increasing the security would have the opposite operation. But His Excellency had considered the circumstances as of such a grave character, and the danger of an attack upon some part of the province sufficiently imminent to warrant immediate action being taken without waiting to consult the House. The entire militia force of the province had, therefore, been turned out.
That was the statement made by Sir Charles Tupper two days after the issue of the proclamation by the Lieutenant Governor. There was great excitement throughout the province at that time, and on the occasion of the next meeting of the legislature, in 1867, there was a discussion as to what did take place', and reports from militia officers as to the number of men who did turn out to drill. The information is given in great detail. I find that the following statement was made by Sir William Fenwick Williams on the opening of the Legislature :
While the colonies have been subjected to threats and in some instances to the invasion of lawless men our province has been exempted from an attack, and although our local forces nobly responded to the call that was made upon them at the early part of the year to arm for the purpose of defence, happily no necessity occurred to require their services to repel an invader.
The exigencies of the province of New Brunswick rendered it necessary for a time to withdraw a large portion of Her Majesty's troops from this garrison for the protection of that colony-
My hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) led us to believe that the people of New Brunswick were looking after themselves but it appears that the regular forces of Nova Scotia were withdrawn and sent over to New Brunswick for the purpose of protecting the frontier of that province.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: Also two companies of militia, the Shubenaoadie and one more, and some volunteers from Halifax.

Sir William Fenwiek-Williams continues:
__and it was with the utmost satisfaction that
I was enabled to fill their places for garrison duty by portions of the Halifax volunteer and militia artillery and the volunteer battalion and to mark how well that service was performed. The readiness and good discipline of the officers and men who were then employed showed how much has been effected by the efforts made during the last years to place our

local forces in a proper condition and how much we can depend upon them in the hour of need.
That shows the response that was made to the call. My Object in reading these extracts is to show the House and the country that in so far as Nova Scotia is concerned the veterans did their duty and if any recognition is going to be given they deserve to share in it. The Historical Society of Nova Scotia has collected a lot of information in regard to this matter and if any gentleman chooses to look at this book which I have in my hand, he will see a picture of the Sydney Mines volunteers in their regimentals, and with their guns at their sides, drilling in 1866, and preparing to resist the invasion. My hon. friend (Mr. 'Carvell), runs away with the idea that they did not turn out at all, but here is a photograph which shows that in one section at least they were drilling on that occasion.
How many men were in the (photograph?

You can count them yourself; there is a very great number of men. There is a paragraph in this historical statement that I would like to read to the minister. It shows that prior to 1866, in the years 1863, 1864 and 1865, very great activity existed in Nova Scotia in militia affairs.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: Forty-four thousand drilled in one year.

I find in this volume, published by the. Nova Scotia Historical Society, the following:
Much good work was done during this year (1864) towards maintaining and improving the force. The counties were divided into regimental districts; the officers and non-commissioned officers were brought into closer touch with the men under their command; the appointment of regimental adjutants was made one of competition, not of favour; and the position of commanding officer of a regiment was conditional on his efficiency, and not necessarily on his seniority in the corps. On 30th June, 105 regiments appeared on the roll, with a total strength of 48,675 officers and men; six months later this had grown to 110 regiments embracing 56,111 of all ranks.
Showing that the militia force of Nova Scotia at that date was very large indeed, compared with the population of the province. If there are 15,000 now in Nova Scotia it would not be a wonderful thing, because 1866 is only forty-eight years ago, and every man who was sixteen years of age was liable to be called out to drill. In my province, where people live to a

ripe old age, it is not surprising that out of 56,000 who did actually drill at that time there should be 15,000 living to-day. I do not agree with the statement that young men have been applying for. this bounty. That is not the case in the constituency I represent, and I never heaird of it in the . province of Nova Scotia.
I want to draw the attention of the minister to the provision with regard to the widows of the veterans. The Bill provides for payment of the bounty to the widows of the veterans who were living on the 1st day of April, 1912. I tsee no good reason why it should be limited to the widow's of veterans who were then alive. It appeals to me that surviving widows of veterans who died prior to that date have the same right to the bounty as the widows of veterans who were living on the 1st day of April, 1912. Early in the present session I put a question on the Order Paper asking what the view of the minister was in regard to this matter, and he was kind enough to give me an answer which I interpreted to mean that he would make provision for the case of these widows.

How many of them
would there be in Nova Scotia?

I was surprised, however, when I read the resolution, to find that it did not contain any such provision.
I asked the minister:
Has the Government considered the advisability of amending the Fenian Raid Volunteer Bounty Act so as to make provision for the payment of the bounty to the widows of veterans who departed this life prior to 1912?
Here is his reply:
Mr. SAM. HUGHES. The Act will be amended if necessary to meet every case that is not settled yet.
The cases of these widows are cases that are not settled yet, and I expected that the minister would make provision for them. I suppose that inadvertently he overlooked it and I hope that before the resolution is finally passed he will deal with this matter.

The hour is late, but I cannot let the resolution pass without saying a word with reference to the position of affairs in the city of Stratford,
12 m. in the riding I have the honour to represent, with regard to this matter. At the time of the Fenian raid there was in Stratford what was known as the Grand Trunk Brigade, a body of very estimable

men, some of whom are still living but a great many of whom have passed to their reward. Those who are living are looking, not for reward, but for like recognition for their services as that accorded to others. The wording of this amendment is very broad, and it would apply to those who were called out to drill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Both amendments
have been ruled out of order, and the main resolution is now before the committee.

In the case of the Nova Scotia veterans, they appear to have been called out by some authority which is not clearly defined, but in the case of the Grand Trunk Brigade of Stratford, the men not only drilled but they went into active service and travelled seventy miles to the American border at Port Huron, defended the lines of communication, and put in all the service that any soldier could perform, until the trouble was over. I have nothing to say against the case of the Nova Scotia veterans, but here is a case which equitably is a much stronger one on which to appeal for recognition. The Stratford men went out as soldiers, performed their duties until all was over, and then were disbanded. J have fought it out with the minister, but he is obdurate. I have not been able to make any headway with him yet, and I give him credit for standing to his guns, but I hope that after hearing my statement to-night he will reconsider the matter. The men who were called out in Nova Scotia merely went to the market square and drilled, but as they were called out by virtue of a proclamation which happens to fit in under the peculiar wording of the Act, they are to be recognized. Surely a brigade like the Grand Trunk Brigade of Stratford, with the regulation uniform, the regulation arms, all the equipment required, going into active service, travelling seventy miles from their homes, and defending their country, ought to be recognized in this legislation?
On what ground does the minister decline to recognize such a fair claim?

Because the men were not regularly called out by duly constituted authority. The point he makes is that they were not part of a military unit or regiment, and unfortunately in Ontario there were no such wide and generous terms of proclamation as in Nova Scotia. In justice to my constituents, I must call the attention of the minister to this particularly hard case, which discriminates against men who are splendid citizens of Canada to-day. I would ask the minister to see that some legislation be enacted which will provide, that in equity the men who went into active service and who discharged their duty faithfully to their Sovereign and their country, should have their loyalty and patriotism recognized.
There was also recognized in my county at that time	and enrolled for the
defence of the country what was known as the Crosshill Company of Millbank, many of the members of which belonged to North Perth, and some to North Waterloo. These men drilled, they were advanced some distance towards the front, and then recalled. In Nova Scotia men who went to the market square by virtue of a proclamation are to get their reward, but in the cases to which I draw attention the men who actually went on active service are to be left out in the cold. Probably it is too late to amend the law this session, but I ask the minister in all candour to give it serious consideration and for the nonce to relax that strict military discipline which actuates him and to let his heart soften so that he may bring these men under the terms of some legislation which will give them that reward which is given to others who performed less service in defence of their country.

The hour is so late that I feel like apologizing for speaking on this question, but I cannot let the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) go without expressing my disapproval of them. The hon. member for Carleton is usually sane and clothed in his right mind, but to-night I think he has gone to the other extreme. There are about 800 applicants for the Fenian Rai'd bounty from the county which I have the honour to represent, and I do not know of a single applicant whose claim is not valid and just and right. I should certainly not wish to think otherwise. If the volunteers of Nova Scotia turned out in such large numbers in 1866, and ran the risk of losing their lives and leaving widows and orphans behind them, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) should not be so severe on them. If the militiamen of New Brunswick, when they found the danger at their door, had taken to the woods, I am sure nobody could find any fault with them if they did not get the bounty which the Minister of Militia is voting for them.

I wish to urge upon the Minister of Militia the advisability of having this bounty paid as quickly as possible. These men are getting very old. Some of the volunteers in the county of Yarmouth are very old indeed. Several of them during this last year have been in very poor circumstances; and, if they had this bounty last fall, it would, no doubt, have prolonged their lives for a time and have prevented some of them from going to the poor asylum, where they died a few weeks after going there. There are otheT cases of death which have occurred since the bounty should have been paid. The minister is open -to censure for not having the bounty paid in the county of Yarmouth when the bounties for the other counties were paid, and I do not see any valid reason why the payment to the volunteers of the county of Yarmouth should have been delayed so long. The minister is also open to censure for not having brought this resolution to the attention of the House before. It should have been brought down before so that these bounties could have been paid before the Easter holiday,
I wish also to refer to the payment of claims of the widows of the veterans who died previous to the passing of the Act in April, 1912. I see no reason why the widows of these volunteers who came out and drilled and were prepared to go to the front, if necessary, should not he entitled to the bountv as much as widows of the men who lived until April 1, 1912. I trust the minister will amend the Act in such a way that the widows of these men may be paid the bounty.
I wish to call the attention of the minister to a circular issued in the county of Yarmouth, dated Chegoggin, N.S., December 2, 1913. I may say that Chegoggin is in the county of Yarmouth. The circular, which is addressed to the Fenian Raid veterans whose claims had been approved at that date, reads as follows:
I have received from Ottawa a list of the applications for the Fenian Raid volunteer bounty that went in from Yarmouth county previous to September 1. Your application has been approved together with about six hundred others from this county. There are thousands of cheques to be issued to Fenian Raid veterans in different counties, which involves a very large amount of extra labour on the Finance Department; but as soon as your turn is reached, your cheque will be mailed to you in a registered letter direct from Ottawa. Congratulating you on the success of your application and wishing you the compliments of the season.
I am.
Yours faithfully,
Howard W. Corning.

Had Mr. Corning any authority from the Department of Militia to send that circular to the Fenian Raid veterans of my county?

Neither directly nor indirectly did any Liberal or any Conservative get any information from the Department of Miilitia concerning any of these names until the papers were laid on the table, and they got nothing except those papers, with one exception, namely, that I spoke to the Prime Minister and gave him data on a certain matter which does not concern the question before the House. Any man who attended the courts of Nova Scotia could have taken down a list of every man whose claim was approved. I have received similar circulars; and when I took my officers to task, they assured me that nothing had been given out by them, but that- representatives of newspapers had been .sitting in the courts at the time and had checked off the names as the claims were approved. I do not wish to waste the time of the House on such a trivial matter.

The answer of the minister is the same as the reply he gave to a question which I put in this House on March 18, of this year. The minister calls it a very trivial matter. I think it is not a trivial matter when Mr. Corning sends out this circular and makes statements which cannot be verified.
In the third paragraph of the circular Mr. Coming says:
There are thousands of checks to be issued to Fenian Raid veterans which involves a very large amount of extra labour on the Finance Department, but as soon as your turn is reached your check will be mailed you in a registered letter direct from Ottawa.
This led the Fenian Raid applicants in the county of Yarmouth to believe that they were to get their checks at once. On December 30, after this circular had been mailed by Mr. Corning, the payments ceased and no further bounties were paid. This caused a great deal of trouble to the applicants in the county of Yarmouth. Many of the men, expecting to get their checks at once, purchased goods or borrowed money, and have been unable up to the present time to repay those from whom they got these favours. The minister is quite right in saying that the Conservatives in the county of Yarmouth are making all the political capital they can out of this matter. I think it is absolutely wrong that the money of the people of Canada should he used for political purposes under the guise of loyalty to these veterans and to their widows.

Permit me to say farther that the report circulated by the Conservatives in Yarmouth and other counties that I voted against the Fenian Rail bounties is absolutely untrue.
I am in favour of these bounties and I hope that payments will be made to the veterans as soon as possible.

The remarks made by
the hon. member for Yarmouth bear out my assertion that this matter is nothing but a game o| polities. The minister himself has said that it is a political matter; let the politicians in Nova Scotia fight it out among themselves. To-day 800 men in the county of Yarmouth claim to have been members of the militia 48 years ago. I want to oppose for all I am worth the suggestion of the hon. member for Guysborough that the widows of the veterans should receive bounties. I think this thing has gone far enough; when you have paid nearly every man who was born in the province of Nova Scotia forty-eight years ago $100, it seems to me that you ought not to pay the widows. The hon. member for Yarmouth spoke about the people of Nova Scotia rallying to the flag and drilling to protect their homes and firesides against invasion. How on earth does my hon. friend think that that band of lawless persons in the neighbouring republic were going to attack Nova Scotia? The whole fleet of the United States at that time consisted of only a few old wooden hulks, and the whole British navy was ready to protect the province of Nova Scotia against invasion by sea. The hon. member for Yarmouth talked as if the people of New Brunswick went to the woods at the time of this raid. I know of a great many people who went to St. Andrews at that time, where there was a possibility of real danger; in my portion of the province of New Brunswick every able-bodied man* responded to the call, and none but those who actually did take part in repelling the invasion are asking to be paid. My father was one of the men who enlisted and if he were alive he would be entitled to a bounty. But I want to point out to my friends from Nova Scotia that my mother is alive and she does not want any $100 from this Government because of what my father did on that occasion. I think it is placing a very small premium upon the loyalty of the people of this country to say that after forty-eight years have passed not only the men but the widows should receive grants; ordinary commonsense should impress upon everybody the fact that these men were but doing their duty.

The hon. member for Guysborough is quite right in resenting the imputation that has been cast upon those persons who have sent claims to the Government for Fenian raid bounties. If the hon. member for Carleton charges that the men who sent in these claims are crooks and perjurers, the Nova Scotia people have a right to resent his imputations in the strongest possible manner. The charges made by the hon. member against a respected body of men in the province of Nova Scotia are the most serious that have been made since I became a member of this House. He has not only insulted the members who have made these applications, but he has insulted the whole province of Nova Scotia. I think there should be an official investigation into the matter, and if the allegations of the hon. member are true, wholesale prosecutions of practically the whole population of Nova Scotia should be made; the men who made these false declarations, as well as the men who helped draw them up and secure the signatures, should be prosecuted. These wholesale accusations made by the hon. member for Carleton should either be proved or withdrawn.

Thirty or forty veterans in the county of Glengarry have made application to the hon. Minister of Militia for this grant. I can cite one case, that of the Hon. A. D. Macdonald, exLieutenant Governor for Ontario who was in a village called Lancaster. He was giving the word as he passed along that the Fenians were coming and that there would likely be an invasion near Lancaster. He sent word to Captain Macdonald, of Alexandria, who sent the word out through Glengarry to bring in volunteers, and before six o'clock in the morning four hundred of our stalwarts arrived in Alexandria with pitchforks ready to defend their country. While I have perhaps not the nerve to appeal to the minister for grants to the men who came with pitchforks to defend their duty, I still feel that he is in a rather awkward and embarrassing position. He is
trying	to	do	his	duty	to	thosewho	are	deserving	and	when	thereaie	so	many	who	are	deserving,	where	is	he	to	draw	the	line ?
I would ask the hon. minister of Militia whether the men who came with pitchforks are not as deserving of the $100 grant as those who came with shot-guns, because they did as much duty as far as the defence of the country is concerned. Therefore I feel that I really should appeal to him to



grant them the $100. We have other cases from Glengarry. I hold in my hand the medal awarded to one of those who perhaps was more deserving according to the argument that has been advanced. Two men, Norman McRae and Sandy McIntosh, who were pals in those days, who marched side by side and heart to heart, ready to shed their blood in defence of Canada, applied for the grant when it was announced that the Government had decided to give $100 to the Fenian raid veterans of '66 and '70. In fact these men were the first of the file claims. Norman McRae was Sandy McIntosh's witness and Sandy McIntosh was Norman McRae's witness. They came together and sent in the application, and the result was that McRae got his $100 but poor Sandy McIntosh has not yet received his. I investigated and found that Sandy's name was not on the pay roll hut Norman's was. I would ask the minister how it was that Norman McRae got his money and Sandy McIntosh did not. Sandy surely was there because I hold his medal in my hand. If the minister figures this out on the basis of the names appearing on the pay roll in order to entitle a man to the grant of $100, it is wrong, because poor Sandy was there with Norman and Norman was there with Sandy. Norman got the grant but Sandy did not. I think myself that we should perhaps remodel the legislation under which these grants are made. There are many good men who did service, even those who came in with their pitchforks, who were ready to do their duty and who are just as much entitled to the grant as those regularly enrolled in the militia. The Government should settle this matter for all time.

We sat very late last night, and the subject of this' resolution is not a matter of contention in any specific way for the sifnple reason that there has been a statute bearing on this matter since 1912. The principle has been recognized that the sum of $100 should be paid by way of bounty to the men who were called out for active service in the years 1866 and 1870. Under the terms of that Act, chapter 53 of II. George V., the time within which these applications could be made in order to take advantage of this Act was December 31, 1913. The minister has now asked the House to extend that time. Practically that is all that is involved in this resolution. In regard to the terms of the resolution, I would point out that there are some things that should be amended. My bon. friend

provides for the grant of $100 to every volunteer who i's living at the date of the passing of the Act based on this resolution. In view of the fact that in the latter portion of the resolution, in the grant which he makes to widows, that grant is made to the widows of volunteers alive on the 1st of April, 1912, that being the date upon which the Act of two years ago was passed. I think the minister should amend this Act so as to make the money payable to the volunteer who was living on the 1st day of April, 1912, because subsequently he goes on to provide for the payment of the money to the widows or legal representatives of the volunteers who died since that time. As a matter of good drafting, I think that should be done.
I would point out to the minister that I think in the great majority of cases that would be affected by this resolution, the applications are on file in the department, and were on file previous to the 31st of December, 1913. The number of cases in which the grant has not been applied for must be very few, and all purposes would be met by the minister limiting the time for the payment of this money to the end of this present year.
Having regard to every question involved, I think it would toe bettor to have this question settled during this year because otherwise, ini view of the expectations which have been raised ini the minds of those who Viovo sent in Their applications, there would be a great deal of dissatisfaction. I would like to ask the minister to consider amending the resolution by substituting 1914 for 1915. I would also like him to consider the suggestion made by my hon. friend f.om Guystoorough (Mr. Sinclair) as to the pension for widows and whether the time could not be extended. In view of the fact that the principle of this Bill was agreed to about two years ago, and as it is only asking for extension of time, I think the minister might well consider the suggestions which have been made. I think if the minister Would ask to report progress and consider the suggestions the results would be as well ion the end.

I am somewhat surprised at the character of the speech which has been- made by the hon. member for Pictou. In view of the broad and sweeping character of the allegations made by the hon. member for Carleton, I thought that some one at least of the different members from

Nova Scotia upon that side of the House would have resented those charges against the people of Nova Scotia. Where was the hon. member for North Cape Breton? Why did he sit silent in this House after those charges had been made?
The hon. member has thought it proper to introduce my name. The discussion is not yet closed; there is plenty of time to hear from the member from North Cape Breton.

It is to be hoped that
we will. I am afraid the sort of artillery my hon. friend uses is a little obsolete now; the rough bore is going out of fashion. The hon. member for Carleton is so much in the habit of making charges that he cannot refrain from attacking his own friends. I suppose that accounts for his attack upon the people of Nova Scotia to-night. Is it because my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) sits so close to my hon. friend from Carleton that he is afraid to resent those charges? We have had a speech from the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Law). He took up most of his time abusing two people: Mr. Corning who wa3 fortunate enough to win an election in Yarmouth against the utmost efforts put forth by the hon. member for that constituency, and that, no doubt, is why he feels so sore against him. The remainder of his speech was taken up by an attempt to censure the Minister of Militia for doing what the hon. member for Yarmouth approves of. The only fault he has to find is that it was not done more quickly, so as to keep a lot of people in Yarmouth out of the poorhouse, because he said that was where they were going last winter.
I did not say any such thing.

It seems to me that the people of Yarmouth will not thank the hon. member for his somewhat unfortunate reflection upon the people of that town. But there are other members from Nova Scotia; there is the hon. member for Richmond. He sits quiet in his seat under the sneers of the hon. member for Carleton.
The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. McKay) did not give me a chance to speak.

I am glad the hon. member still has the use of his speech, which we have often heard in this House-not 213i
often with pleasure. I had hoped that some of those members would have resented the charges made by the hon. member for Carleton against the people of Nova Scotia. The junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) sits silent in his seat under those reproaches. If some member on this side of the House had made that statement in regard to the 15,000 good men and true of the province of New Brunswick-men who did not shed any blood but probably shed some sweat drilling in the market place-and had called those men perjurers because, inferentially, that is what they were called by the hon. member for Carleton, what a row there would have been! I am surprised at the. junior member for Halifax, and pained as; well, because I did think that with all his faults (which he possesses in a high degree) there was in him some loyalty to the people of his native province. The people of Nova Scotia are not perjurers, I know they are honest men. The generation of 1866 was loyal, and so are their descendants, but so have their representatives in this House fallen that they will permit' the hon. member for Carleton to insult them, and yet not one will lift his voice in protest. We have seen the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) wax eloquent in this House in regard to Nova Scotia and its people, yet he was as mild as any sucking dove when he got up to speak. Where have all the fireworks gone? Is the stock exhausted that we did not have an exhibition from the member for Pictou to-night? We might have expected him to hurl back in the very teeth of the gentleman who sits behind him the charges that that hon. member distributed so plentifully with regard to the people of Nova Scotia. Not only has my hon. friend charged the people of that province with perjury, but he has, inferentially, charged the members from Nova Scotia who have been supporting the claims of those people with what you may call subornation or perjury. Gentlemen opposite are as much guardians of the treasury as those who sit on the Treasury benches, yet these representatives are trying to get these bounties granted to people who, my hon. friend says, are not entitled to them. They are helping to rob the treasury of these various $100 bounties against the best interests of the country. I hope some members from Nova Scotia upon that side of the House will do their duty.
What about that side?

Members upon this side can always be depended upon to do their duty, but surely the first to spring to their feet should be members on the side from which the hon. gentleman comes who makes the charges. They have failed, and I have no doubt that we will hear from some gentlemen on this side from Nova Scotia.

I was not willing at first to butt into the merry little family quarrel that has been going on on the other side of the House, but inasmuch as I represent a Nova Scotia constituency, and inasmuch as the hon. gentleman who is the offender in this respect evidently expects some remarks from this side of the House, I cannot resist the temptation of making a statement, although the hour is somewhat late. In the first place, I shall refer very briefly to the remarks of the hon. member for Kings, Prince1 Edward Island (Mr. J. J. Hughes). I think we all sympathized with him in the plea he put forward for the payment of claims to the citizens of Prince Edward Island, even though, a- he himself explained, the claims of those people for the bounty are very slight indeed.

I made no such
statement.
I understood the'effect of the hon. gentleman's speech to be that the citizens of Prince Edward Island, who had turned out to drill in 1866, should be paid the bounty.

You are correct in the sense that they would not come under the provisions of the resolution when the minister insisted upon them being called out by proclamation, but they were just as well entitled to receive this consideration as the men in any other province of the Dominion.

That is really what I
wanted to say, but I have not the facility of speech that my hon. friend has and perhaps the House will pardon me if my remarks are somewhat obscure. The point I wish to make is that it seems somewhat regrettable that when this hon. gentleman was sitting on this side of the House, and when the party of his own political persuasion was in power, he do not take the same 'interest in this question. Not only did he not make a proposition of this kind when his own party was in power, not only did he not lift his voice for his constituents, but he

actually voted against a proposition of this kind. When a gentleman on our side of the House, then in Opposition, advocated the payment of bounties to the Fenian Raid veterans, my hon. friend voted against any proposition of that kind.
Tell me when that took place?

It was in the year of
our Lord 1906. If my hon. friend looks at page 614 of 'Hansard' of 1906 he will see that Mr. F. D. Monk moved the following resolution:
That It Is desirable that the Government of Canada should recognize in some substantial manner the services rendered during the Fenian raids of 1866 and 1870 by our Canadian volunteers.
Mr. Hughes' name is recorded as one of those who voted against that resolution. I was not only shocked but I was absolutely pained at the very unwarranted remarks which were made to night by my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell). My hon. friend actually states that 15,000 of the good people of Nova Scotia perjured themselves.

I want my hon. friend
to withdraw that statement because I did not make it.
A big proportion.

No, nor a big proportion. I asked this House if they believed there were 15,000 men old enough to have been members of the militia at that time. I did not say that they had all perjured themselves. I always stand by What I say and it is not for the hon. gentleman to attribute to me something that I did not say.
What did you say?
The hon. gentleman can read what I said, and he can take his own meaning out of it.

I do not want to put
words into the mouth of the hon. gentleman that he does not utter because there is no necessity of doing that. I understood him to say that this was a stupendous farce, that it was absurd.

Yes. What does the
hon. gentleman mean by saying that I have not always advocated the payment of these bounties?

I will try to explain.
In the year of our Lord 1906 the hon. gentleman was in the House representing the county of Guysborough. A resolution was proposed which I have already read, by an hon. member, Mr. Monk. On that occasion did the hon. member foT Guysborough vote for Mr. Monk's resolution?

Mr. Monk's resolution
had no reference whatever to the payment of $100 to the Fenian Raid veterans. I understood the resolution referred to a land grant.	[DOT]

These are the w'ords:
That it is desirable that the Government of Canada should recognize in some substantial manner the services rendered during the Fenian Raid of 1866 and 1870 by our Canadian volunteers.
Is there anything there about a land grant?

If you will read the
speech you will find he did refer to land grants and nothing but land grants.
I am not reading the speech. I am reading the resolution-the thing that was voted on.
Was there an amendment to that resolution?

And the hon. gentleman (Air. Sinclair) in 1906 voted against that resolution which did not say anything about land grants, and which merely asked that these veterans be rewarded in some substantial way. Furthermore, in the year

1911, my hon. friend from North Grey (Mt. Middlebro) proposed substantially the same resolution, which is to be found at page 9603 ' Hansard ':
That it is desirable that the Government of Canada should recognize in some substantial manner the services rendered during the Fenian raids of 1866 and 1870 by our Canadian volunteers.
It is seen therefore that some years after the first we have a second resolution and nothing about a land grant in it, and yet the hon. member for Guysborough when his friends were in power voted that they should do nothing to reward the veterans.
I desire positively to contradict the statement made by my hon. friend. I was not present; I was not in the Dominion of Canada at the time that resolution was moved in the House.

I will refer the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sinclair) to page 9634 of
Hansard '. I do not think my hon. friend will repudiate a pair, and I find, among other names on that page, the euphonious name of Sinclair, which I presume means him.
My hon. friend does not find on that page that I voted against the resolution of my hon. friend from North Grey, and if he says so he is not telling the truth.
I will be very glad to hand the book over to my hon. friend.
I was not in the country at the time; I was in England.
The hon. gentleman was paired.
Oh.
Do hon. gentlemen opposite say that pairing is not voting?
Certainly.

Do they say that a pair means nothing? I want to say
1 a.m. that it either means something or that the whip on the Liberal side of the House on that occasion practised the grossest fraud on this side of the House. I am a very young member of this House, but I have been a watchful student of 'Hansard,' and I never found yet an instance in which a member of Parliament denied or repudiated a pail.
He is the first man to do it in the House.
That is not repudiating a pair.

My hon. friend from Guysborough is not alone in this regard, because other members from Nova Scotia, in fact, every single Liberal member who was then representing Nova Scotia, including my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), including my hon. friend from Pietou (Mr. Macdonald)-

Just wait there. I want to say to my hon. friend that he has suppressed the facts in regard to the resolution of 1906. Mr. Monk, In moving the resolution, did not know that there was a Fenian Raid veteran in the province of Nova Scotia, and that resolution was opposed by Sir Frederick Borden, representing the Government, who pointed out to Mr. Monk that Nova Scotia had a large number of veterans whose claims should be taken into consideration. He asked Mr. Monk to withdraw the resolution in order that, the whole question might be inquired into, and we voted against Mr. Monk's resolution because he did not know up to that time that there was a single Fenian Raid veteran i'n Nova Scotia.
Oh.
The noisy brigade over there on the other side do not know-what they are talking a/bout. Furthermore, in regard to 1911-

I am very glad to have my hon. friend endeavour to correct a mistake, but I do not want him to make a speech when-1 am addressing the House. I think he occupies as much of the time of the House as I do, and I do not think he should deny me the little time I am taking now.
If my hon. friend does not want me to correct a mistake in regard to 1911, I shall not make any further reference to it.
Order.
Do I understand that my hon. friend (Mr. Davidson) will permit me to correct a mistake with regard to 1911?
Certainly, you can give your side of the case if you wish.

The hon. gentleman will find a list of pairs on the resolution moved by Mr. Middlebro. This resolution was a purely obstructive motion made on

going into Supply, as everybody knows. At the time the motion was made my hon. friend from Guysborough was in England, and the hon. member (Mr. Davidson) indulges in diatribes against him because his name appears in the list of pairs. I was in Nova Scotia at the time; I was not in the House. I never knew the resolution was moved, and how can I be charged with responsibility?

I am very glad to have the explanation of the hon. member from Pictou, because I do not want to do that hon. gentleman any injustice. He is very careful not to do injustice to anybody else, and I do not want to do injustice to him.
Did I understand the hon. member (Mr. Davidson) to say that every member from the province of Nova Scotia on the Liberal side voted against that resolution in 1911?
Every member on the Liberal side who was in the House.
You did not qualify your statement in that way before.
When this motion was put in 1906, the hon. gentleman appears as voting against it, and he never repudiated the pair until this late hour, when it cannot do him any harm.

I am not down thare as
paired; I defy the hon. gentleman to sliow it.
It i3 ' Mr. Low,' not ' Mr. Law.'
We will find out about that.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davidson) had better get on another pair of glasses if he wants to find my name there. I call on him to apologize for his statement.
Oh.

I ask him to withdraw the
statement. It is absolutely untrue. It has been stated in Yarmouth and in other counties ovar and over again by Conservatives. The statement is a wilful and deliberate lie. I ask the hon. gentleman, if he is a gentleman at all, to withdraw the statement.'

I am very sorry that
my hon. friend (Mr. Law) has shown so much heat, because really it is a case where
he has to take back water, not I. If he will look at page 647 of ' Hansard,' 1906, he will find Ms name is there, L-A-W, and while I would like to accommodate my hon. friend and take back any statement displeasing to him, yet as a good constitutional member of this House I am bound to stand by the records, and now I am going to ask my hon. friend from Yarmouth to take back the statement he made.

I say I did not vote, and my name is not there as voting, but it may be there as a pair.
Mr. DAVIDSON. The statement I made was that the .hon. gentleman appeared as a nair and he said he did not.
Read the record as it is and let us have it all.

You will find it at
page 647.
We have not all got that volume of ' Hansard ' here.
There are a great many names of Nova .Scotia Liberal members who either voted or were paired.

Give us the names of
those who voted and those who weTe paired.

It is really too much bother to pick them out but they are there. My hon. friend from Pictou, and my hon. friend" from Yarmouth, .and my hon. friend from Guysborough come forward now when their party is not in power, notwithstanding the fact that they appear as voting against this proposition, when their own party was in power, and they now say, when they are in opposition and when they have no responsibility, that we on this side have not gone far enough. They say that we should pay not only those who were alive in the year 1912, and the widows of those who have died since that date., but the widows of all Fenian Raid veterans and their children. All hon. members opposite deplored that the Minister of Militia was so slow and dilatory in making these payments. Had my hon. friends opposite stood to the back of Mr. Monk in 1906, or to the back of the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middle-bro), in the year 1911 and forced their Government to enact legislation such as we enacted the moment we got into power, then these people would not have had to wait so long; they would have all been paid and a great many widows, whose bus-

bands have died since 1906, in all these counties would also have been paid. Hon. gentlemen opposite cut a very peculiar figure at the present time. When their party was in power, they were very careful as to what obligations their Government would assume; but when they are in opposition, when their words are merely as idle tales, then they are very generous. They remind me of a Bible story. It is recorded in Holy Writ how Lazarus begged alms of Dives in this world and although Dives, when he was alive and had the pull, would not give Lazarus a crumb, after he went to his reward he became very full of concern for his relatives. This is one letter, of which I have scores in my desk, which has been -sent out to veterans in Nova Scotia:
My Dear Sir:

I would like the hon. gentlemen to explain what particular energies they displayed in order to make these bounties payable.

At the time that the1 Fenian Raid Bounty Act was passed, about the 1st of April, 1912, my hon. friend from Annapolis was a member of this House and I have no doubt that he was in his place at the time when this question was asked by myself. Mr. Sinclair:	Will the Act apply to men

Mr. Hughes (Victoria) : The law says they must have been called out for active service and the man who is called out for drill is not called out for active service. He has to he called out in anticipation of meeting the enemy.
