When this Act went upon the statute book members representing Nova Scotia constituencies, who were in the habit of conferring together with regard to these matters, were receiving a large number of letters from Fenian Raid veterans inquiring as to the possibility of their obtaining the bounty. Upon looking et the Act we found that it applied only to those persons who had been called out for actual service. The question then arose as to what constituted actual service, and whether or not Nova Scotia veterans could qualify under that Act. We first went to the department, and the department insisted that proof must be given that the Nova Scotia people had actually been called out for active service. said that that was satisfactory. We then, in turn, notified our constituents to that effect.

We notified our constituents in February, 1913. Applications had gone in from various counties, but no bounties had been paid up to the time when the proclamation was discovered. In March, after certain persons had sent copies of the newspapers containing this information to hon. geptlemen opposite, the hon. member for Halifax, the hon. member for Pictou, the hon. member for Guysborough and several other hon. gentlemen opposite rose, with apparent indignation, and criticised us for following this procedure and for appointing commissioners to take these applications. A few weeks afterwards these hon. gentlemen were doing the same thing themselves.
Doing what?

Following the very
course which we pursued.
What course was that?

That of informing their constituents, through the press, that those who were called out under the terms of the proclamation were entitled to the bounty, and the further course of appointing competent and intelligent commissioners in the county to take these applications. That was the course we followed, and that was the course imitated by hon. gentlemen opposite.
Does my hon. friend say that it was in February of 1913, when he first discovered that the veterans of Nova Scotia were sure of obtaining the bounties?
No, I said nothing of the kind. Some time previous to February, 1913, we made the discovery and in that month we wrote the press.

As the Chairman has ruled that an amendment to this resolution cannot be accepted under the rules, I would ask that the minister withdraw the resolution and get the consent of the Governor General to add the province of Prince Edward Island with the others.

The bold and defiant challenge which the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) hurled across the floor of the House to hon. gentlemen on this side has its parallel in the nursery legend of a family in my town. A little boy, two and a half years old, was wearing his first pair of trousers and was very proud of them. He came out on the sidewalk to see if any one would notice them. The butcher came along, stopped his team at the door, and while he was cutting the order of meat which the boy's mother gave, the young fellow stood in front with his hands in his trousers' pockets. The butcher did not notice him. Then the boy went around in front of the horse, looked at the horse and finally said:	'Say, mister, is your
horse afwaid of twousies? ' I wish to say to the hon. member for Annapolis that I am not afraid of his trousers nor of the hon. member who stands in them. Hon. gentlemen express some surpise that the members from Nova Scotia did not protest against what they were pleased to call an imputation upon the honesty and good faith of the people of the province of Nova Scotia who applied for Fenian Raid bounties. I want them to understand that they are not the first men who are willing to stand up in this House and defend the honesty of the people of that province. But I did not understand the hon. member for iCarleton to cast any imputation on the people of Nova Scotia in respect of fraudulent applications for Fenian Raid bounties. What I did understand the hon. membeT for Carleton to say was that it was preposterous that in Nova Scotia the bounty should be given to men who did not go to the front to repel the invaders who threatened the shores of Canada in 1866, men who simply served in the militia at home, whereas the men in New Brunswick who actually left their homes and went to the front to meet the invaders did not receive a single dollar. If the people of Nova Scotia are enjoying the advantage of a bounty of $100 in respect of the service they performed in 1866 then the people of Nova Scotia have very little to thank my hon. friend from Annapolis for or any hon. gentleman supporting the Government in this House. My bon. friend in the course of his observations endeavoured to fasten upon the Liberal members in this House a charge of having voted against remuneration for Fenian Raid bounties in Nova Scotia when in 1906 they voted down a resolution moved by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I desire
to call the attention of the committee to the fact that Mr. Monk's resolution was not for a pension or for a grant of money to compensate these men for their services. His whole argument was in favour of a grant of land to be paid, not to the veterans of Nova Scotia, not to the veterans of New Brunswick, or of Prince Edward Island, but simply to the men who were called out in Ontario and Quebec in 1866.
Will my hon. friend be good enough to show by the resolution of Mr. Monk where.it is stated that it is confined to the people of Quebec?

He never heard of
Nova Scotia having Fenian Raid veterans when he moved the motion.
Mr, DAVIDSON:	I understood the hon.
member to say that what the Nova Scotia Liberal members voted against was that payments should be made not only to citizens of Ontario and Quebec. That, furthermore, it was not for a money payment but for land. I ask him to point out, in the resolution which was voted down, anything to that effect.

It is just the size of the hon. member for Annapolis to endeavour to confine my remarks to the resolution. What I propose to do is to direct the attention of the committee to Mr. Monk's interpretation of the resolution. Mr. Monk said:
As to the kind of acknowledgment to be given, undoubtedly that which has been talked about during these interviews, and prob-bably on that account is most mentioned amongst the veterans, is a grant of land. We have a very large territory still in the hands of the Government which we are endeavouring to settle. It is most desirable that that territory should be settled as soon as possible and with the best sort of people. 1 do not think it would be possible to And better men to undertake the settlement of our great Northwest than these men. Objection has been taken on the ground that there are not only the veterans whose claim I am now urging, hut also other deserving classes. Reference is made to the volunteers, who, in 1885 went up to the Northwest to put down the rebellion there. There were also those who saw active service during the Boer war in South Africa.
He did not even want these veterans to get the land free. He said:
I am advocating, not an absolutely fr'ee grant of land perhaps to those men, but on account of their merits we should acknowledge their services, the fidelity with which they have performed their duties, and at the same time encourage the volunteer movement, which I think should be encouraged in this country.

Reference to the speech of Mr. Monk will show that his resolution wae designed to bring about some recognition for the volunteers in the province of Quebec and in . the province of Ontario. He proceeded:
Scrip might be given to them, quarter-sections might be given to them without conditions and they would do with them what they saw fit, or conditions might be imposed upon them whilst granting them each a quarter-section which would enable them if they would not ensure their own presence on the lands to be settled-because most of them have reached an age when it is to a certain extent impossible for them .to go themselves and settle these lands-to delegate the execution of the restrictions upon them for the settlement and for the final patenting of these lots to members of their own families.
Now, Mr. Monk, in the light of the interpretation which he places on the resolution by his own language, certainly was not seeking support for his resolution from the Liberal members from the province of Nova Scotia. These volunteers in Nova Sooti'a performed their service in 1866. It was forty odd years afterwards that Mr. Monk moved his resolution in this House, and at that stage, when the youngest of these men must have been sixty years of age, the only compensation he desired for them, even if he intended they should benefit by it, was that they should pull up their stakes, leave the homes they had won in Nova Scotia, leave the land which they had cultivated, on which they had brought up their families and go out to the Northwest to take up quarter sections-and even these were not to be free to them.

Under the terms of
that resolution might not $100 be given instead of land?

There is an old story about what might .have happened if something else had not happened. I am only speaking about this resolution. Sir Frederick Borden said on that occasion:
I understood one of his arguments to be that after all, this will not be such a serious matter because there were less than 2,000 of these men living in the province of Quebec and some 10,000 or 12,000 in Ontario.
I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend unnecessarily-

There, we have the crux of the whole matter. We can point to the Bill passed in 1912, which is the subject more particularly of the discussion here this evening. My hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence having been aware that a considerable agitation had developed and continued in Quebec and Ontario for some years in respect to the compensation that ought to be paid to Fenian Raid veterans, considered that the time was opportune to deal with it. and Defence, .like the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, did not have in mind compensating the Fenian Raid veterans of Nova Scotia. The veterans of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were not in his mind at the time; he simply had reference to the veterans of Quebec and Ontario when this Bill was under discussion. 1 quote from 'Hansard,' 1912:
Mr. Currie: Might I ask the minister if it is intended to give the men of 1866 the same amount of pensions for wounds as the 1886 men got?
Mr. Hughes (Victoria) : This is not dealing with pensions at all. That would have to he done by way of special Act.

Mr. Hughes (Victoria) : If a man were called out in active service in either year. Some men were out only a week, and they come in under the Act; some were out three months and they get just the same. It is a thing one cannot possibly equalize in any other way.
Mr. Sinclair : Will the Act apply to men who were called out to drill? Mr. Hughes (Victoria) : The law says they must have been called out for active service and the man who is called out for drill is not called out for active service. He has to be called out in anticipation of meeting the enemy.

There cannot be any question as to what was in the mind of the Minister of Militia and Defence. Another letter reads as follows:
November 1, 1912.
The Act you refer to was passed last winter and referred to those times of the Fenian Raid. Just what the most liberal interpretation of active service means has not been clearly defined, but so far only those who were ir, active engagements or were on the pay roll of the country at the time, are recognized as being entitled to the bounty.
Therefore, as late as November, 1912, seven months after the Act had been passed and received the assent of His Royal Highness, a member as elosely associated with the Minister of Militia as the hon. member for Lunenburg believed in his mind and heart that only those men who went to the front were entitled to the Fenian Raid bounty. I think I have some more proof as to what men higher up in the councils of the Government believed. Last session of Parliament the following question was asked the Right Hon. R. L. Borden by Mr. Sinclair:

In order to be living to-day they must have been living then. Then, section 4 reads:
